heart was the belief that she herself with all her faults and failings was dearest on earth to the Earl of Alandale, How would it end?
Sir John stared at her in amazement rot a moment, then as he thought over things it occurred tO him that if he knew the murderer's name Mr. Fielding could hunt up proofs and details.

" I think he would turn Mc out OI CIOOIS and never speak to me again." Sir John looked thoughtfully at the girl. "You have my promise,' he said very gravely, "and I need not tell you I shall keep my word. Unless you give me your full and free consent, I will tell no one whence I de- rived my information. In return will you suffer me to tell Fielding—poor Alandale's lawyer—that I have received information which convinces me the crime Was committed by someone from Australia, presumably a former lover of Miss Jardine ? " - "I don't think that could do ariy harm," agreed Maria, "and, of course, if there was actually no other way of saving Lord Alan- dale's life I' would come forward at the trial and tell all I know. But I shbuld have such a terrible time with my father, and I don't want to do that if it can attyhow be helped." "I will remember," said Sir John. "Now, Miss Mackenzie, you and I must meet some- times to consult together about this business. I gather it would offend Mr. Mackenzie if I were to call at Rockmount ? " " It would never do atvall."

Her will was good to save Kenneth even by the confession of her sin, but would the fact that she was not his cousin but an imposter help to clear Lord Alandale of the charge of murder ? Helen doubted it; she believed the case against him would look even blacker still if it were once noised abroad that she had been the wife of the murdered man.

"Yours are hard terms," he told Maria gravely, "but things are so desperate with my friend I will agree to them." "It was Helen Jardine." "Miss Jardine—impossible 1" " I am sure of it," said Maria ; " I—l was so interested in the case that I went out alOne. one night to look for the revolver. Well, I found it, and it had the name of a Melbourne tradesman engraved on it. Sir John, Helen Jardine is the only person in these parts who has 'lately come from Australia." "Have you told anyone of this ? " " No. I wrote to Mi. Fielding anony mously, telling him it was of no use his offering a reward for the revolver because I had found it and that I would only produce it when there seemed no other hope of saving Lord Alan- dale's life."
People with evil minds would declare that Alandale loved her so madly he had taken the life of the man who stood between them.

"You will stay -here, won't you " Helen pleaded to Magdalen. " Oh! please don't go away; you will be such a comfort to Lady Mary, and it does me good even to hear you speak, because poll think there is still a chance of Kenneth's being acquitted. As for me I as if I had no hope left and all was dark despair." = "I am going to Aunt Mary now," said Magdalen. "If she is willing, I shall be glad to stay at Alandale for a little while ; I think it is easier to bear the suspense here on the spot where one hears each fresh detail of the case."

"And you found it—when ? " "About a month ago, between the first and second meeting of the magistrates" "If only you had gone to Fielding and taken the revolver with you," groaned Sir John, "think of all the suffering that might have been spared Lord Alandale. This is, of course, if it is the weapon really used."

"Then I must think of some other plan," said Sir John thoughtfully. "Any way, Miss Mackenzie, you and I are friends and we must see more of each other." Maria shook hands with the baronet and went home easier in mind than she had felt for many a weary day.

Helen slept that night as she had not done since Lord Alandale's arrest ; it seemed as though Magdalen's very presence had brought her hope and comfort, besides which Mag- dalen acted as a sort of " buffer " between the heiress and Lady Mary. A great favourite with the latter she made her see that it was simply cruelty to blame Helen for the course of events.

Maria shivered. " There's no doubt about that," she said in a troubled tone ; " I found a handkerchief, too, and that was stained with blood. I could not go to Mr. Fielding for two reasons, my father would never have forgiven me, and— well, I've seen Lord Alandale and his cousin together, and I'm pretty sure by the way he looked at her then he'd rather suffer anything himself than that her guilt should be dis- covered."

"She is as much cut up as we are," wound up Magdalen, "and can't you see that merely the very fact of her presence here having brought that misbrable Norton to the village adds terribly to her grief ? " EMI% Fielding felt more harassed and dis- tressed than he had ever done in the whole of his professional life. The impenetrable mystery which at first shrouded the murder had been easier for him to bear than the knowledge he now possessed —or believed he possessed. The anonymous letter had dons its work and made him positive Helen Jardine was the murderer, and though he felt inclined to b - lieve the vague promise in the letter that a confession would be made When no other way remained of saving Lord Alandale's life, that promise did not comfort him.

"But Miss Jardine could not have been guilty," said Sir John Leigh ; " the evidence of the revolver with the Australian makers' —seller's rather—name would clear Lord Alandale, but it could not condemn her."

"Why not ? " "Perhaps von are a stranger in this place and do not gnow the story of Miss Jardine's miraculous escape. Well, the truth of it is that the ship she sailed in from Australia caught fire and Miss Jardine was rescued from the blazing vessel after she had lost all hope of escaping with her life. .She and others 'were taken on board by a large pleasure yacht and they had absolutely nothing with them but

He construed it to meverethat the trial wo ild be allowed to take place, that the Earl wjild go through all Ihe agony and humiliation ol being sentenced :to death and might then be saved at the eleventh hour by a confession that would make him miserable for the rest of his life. To Mr. Fielding's mind the confesFion should have been made at once, sand there were times when he thought of telling Helen Jardine so with his own lips. In those days he (to quote the opinion of his partner) neglected other clients shamefully and seemed to devote his whole time and thought to the Alandale murder; he was so often backwards and forwards that Mr. Mait- land said mockingly he had better take a season ticket between Thomby and York; his wife saw less of him at this time ,than at any other period of their married life, and even Mr.'Arnot, devoted friend as he was to all the house o 4 Jardine, told his son-in-law he took the race too much to heart.
"You are doing all that strength and will and intellect can for poor Alandale," he said to Joe; "why can't, you rest content and leave the rest to God ? "
CHAPTER XVIII.

IT must not be supposed that Miss Macken- zie forgot her nocturnal search in the Alandale grounds and the discovery she made there. Maria was not the type of character to " for- get f' so startling an adventure; she had be- lieved that when once her letter to Mr. Field- ing was seni she could "put The matter out of 4er head " for a little, but to her surprise she 'oand it impossible. Morning, • noon, and night the thought of Lord Alandale, imprisoned for his cousin's crime, simply haunted her, and if she had not happened to be of a very strong constitution and clear healthy brain, she would certainly have worried herself into a nervous fever. As it was she grew so silent and absent-minded that her mother became ,seriously alarmed and even ventured to hint to her imperious lord and master that "Maria wanted a change." • "Well, she can't have one till after Septem- ber, so it's no use her wanting it, "Said the iron- master decidedly. " I mean to stay here till after Lord Alandale's trial. I couldn't miss fiearing the verdict for anything. And as to trusting you to take the girl away, I could not think out ; you'd let her get engaged to the first whipper snapper of a clerk who took a fancy to my money and pretended he was in love with her." ,

Mrs. Mackenzie sighed but gave up the con- test; she had not much spirit, poor woman, and the little she had was easily quelled. " It's no use," /she said sadly to her daugh- ter; "your pa won't ,hear of our going away without him and he's set on staying here till after the Hamborough Assizes." • And at those words and the thought of the man whose fate was to be decided Maria actually amazed her mother by bursting into tears. She was ashamed of her own grief and would not answer one of Mrs. Mackenzie's questkins, but declared she was " tired" and the heat tried her ; she obstinately denied that there was " anythime on her mind," and finally, as the shortest way of ending the dis- cussion, she put on her things and went out for a walk.

She chose the woods which lay between her own home and Alandale as the scene of her promenade. There was a public footpath through them, but it was very little used, and when Maria sat down on a fallen tree to "have a think," as she would have called it, she be- lieved there was not the least chance of her being disturbed. But she was mistaken; a man strolling through the wood with his dog came suddenly face to face with her ; the, animal, a collie puppy, not having arrived at the age of dis- cernment, mistook Maria for a friend and pro- ceeded to fawn on her With the boisterous affection of his puppy nature so the owner naturally had to call him off, wondering in his mind at the same time who the handsome girl could possibly be. Sir John Leigh had been abroad for over two years and had not been home many months; he knew Peter Mackenzie from meet- lag him on the magistrates' bench, but he had never met his wife or daughter ; in fact, he was hardly likely to seeing that the' iron- master's family were hardly yet " reeeiv.el " into society except on sufferance, while Sir John ,was courtbd assiduonsly by all the neighbourhood as the last of the 'good old name and the best match in the district. He thought Maria a " monstrous tine girl," but•he was certainly a little surprised when she addressed him by name. . "You are Sir John Leigh," she said frankly. " Is it true that you are a great friend of Loi:d Alandale ? " " Quite true," said Sir John irankly, "and " I never spoke to him in my life," Maria, " but I should very much like to ialk to you about the murder ion could spat, me a little of your time." Sir John's answer was to sit down by ILIS herside on the fallen tree and 'to assure hert time was quite at her disposal. To do the baronet justice he would have interviewed- a female Methuselah if he thought it likely to profit his friend, but he decidedly preferied talking to this very handsome if unconven- tional young lady. " I'm in a dreadful fix," said Maria. " I know who killed that man but I can't ticcie sdiether to tell anyone." "My dear young lady." cried Sir John. " if you can help us to light on the real niurilt'n.•r, it is your bounden duty to do So ; I cann.ii understand your hesitating." "I don't mind telling you," said Mull with a flattering emphasis on the pronoun ‘') which she was quite uncoircious, " but you must promise me first not to tell anyone wllere you got your information."
my story tienneln may De set at liberty at once and not have to go to Hamborough at all ? "
Magdalen • attempted no more argument with her cousin, but when Mr. Fielding arrived she had a word alone with him. •

I am certain Helen is so upset she isn't answerable for her action's." And she went on to tell him her cousin's plan. Joe Fielding looked very sad. "To my mind she should have done it long ago. Miss Magdalen, I know you • will be angry with me, but I have felt sure for some weeks past Miss Jardine was the guilty person." "Then you made the greatest mistake of your life. At least be kind to her, Mr. Field- ing, don't let her see from your face or manner the cruel thing 3,-oki think of her." It waS an almost silent drive; they were within five. minutes of the prison before Helen spoke at all, then she asked : _ _ . _ _ _
"Is it trim that Lord Alandale will be re- moved to Hamborough. to-morrow ? " "We expect so."

"Then I'm glad I came to-day. You must let me see him quite alone, please. How long may I stay with him ? " a Half .an hour," answered Fielding. I As a fact Lord Alanilale: not being a con- victed prisoner the time might have been longer, but the lawyer knew ,a little of what anguish the meeting might cause his client and was anxious to cut the intc?rviw short. " I will wait for you," he told Helen with grave courtesy, as she left him under the guidance of a warder. " Don't trouble. I can drive home alone."
" I would rather wait," replied Mr. Field- ing; "as it happens I have an appointment here Shortly with Sir. John Leigh."

"That man," and -a sneer-rose to Helen's lips, " he is a false friend and turncoat." She was allowed to enter the cell alone, and the door was locked On her. It was not foroperly a cell at all, for as an unconvicted prisoner Lord Alandale had been allowed to pay for somewhat better accommodation; it was in fact a bare-looking square room with whitewashed -walls on • which the sunbeams danced, and the window, though heavily barred; looked out on .the courtyard. There was very little furniture, a narrow bed, the plainest Of toilet' apparatus,.•and One wooden chair, but Helen noticed nothing of the sur- roundings, all she saw was the face of .the prisoner, the man she loved. A little thinner and graver than in the early summet days

CHAPTER XVII.

Ma. FIELDING felt' that fate was indeed against him when the time came for the second appearance of Lord Alandale before the Thomby Bench of magistrates; he had hoped . and believe that a further adjournment would be made, but to his surprise and dis- may the day's sitting ended in the committal of the Earl for trial at the Hamborough Assizes. In plain English, seven weeks hence Kenneth. Lord Alandale, would be tried for his life,.; al Joe Fielding, who believed in his client's innocence with all his heart, Saw no way of proving it ; while, if he was right in his interpretation of the anonymous letter, and Helen Jardine was, indeed, the murderess, even if she revealed her guilt at the eleventh hour rather than see her cousin suffer, Fielding thought the Earl loved her so intensely that her disgrace would be almost more agony to him than his own. Perhaps Joe Fielding felt his perplexities all the deeper because it was impossible to confide them to anyone ; his partner was so utterly incredulous of Lord Alandale's innocence that they had quite ceased to discuss the case; Mr. Arnot. simple, kindly man, would only have been made wretched by the doubt of Helen's innocence being suggested to him. Joe Fielding felt almost inclined to inter- view Miss Jardine herself, so baffled was he at all points. But the very day that saw Kenneth com- a mitted for trial brought an arrival to the Hall who did much to relieve the heavy tension among the inmates of the grand old house. While Lady Mary • Jardine was shut up in her • own room and poor Helen wandered about aimlessly as one who cannot rest or settle to anything, a statien fly drove slowly up the avenue and the butler greeted the solitary :figure who emerged from it with a strange minture of delight and restraint. "Ott t Miss Magdalen." said the faithful servant, "it does my heart good to see you ; but we are in sore trouble, miss. There!s a shadow on the place." "I know all about it, Giles," said Magdalen simply. "Mother and I were having, a little 7- holiday abroad and so I did not hear of all that was happening here till two days ago, then I left her to travel slowly and cattle back as fast as steam could bring me. And now will you take me to my cousin? " • Giles looked as though he disliked the task. "Lady Mary would be 4oinforted to see : you, miss," he began deprecatingly, and-" ; '• And my cousin is a stranger. I know just what you arc thinking, but because she is a stranger she must sorely need comforting. Show me to her at once." Helen looked up in bewilderment at the sight of a tall, slender figure in .a hat and ! travelling dress; she guessed who it must be, ! but she was not left to conjecture. Magdalen : went up to her with outstretched hand " We meet in troubled times, Helen ; I was abroad when I heard the bad news, but I could not stay away." She would :have kissed the heiress, but to . her surprise Helen drew back as though to evade the embrace. "If you have heard the true account you must blame me," she said in a voie that was harsh with pain; "everyone here Aes. After the examination closed .this afternkon Aunt Mary said she' hoped I was satisfied with my work.' Oh, Magdalen, my very heart is breaking with the thought of Kenneth's peril, but just because I am almost a stranger to him, because. a few months ago we had never ! • met, no one believes me." "I believe you," said Magdalen, putting an ! arm round the other girl in spite of her reluctance and drawing her to herself with a caressing touch which was wonderfully motherly in one so young. " I believe you implicitly. Heler, and now I want you to sit down and tell me all about it ; I have only heard the newspaper report s.s vet." "Then perhaps you don't know the worst. Alandale was committed for trial • this after- noon.:' "Yes, I know that ; it was on the placards ot the special rapers the newsboys 7 were crying at the station." You must be tired and worn out after your journey," said Held wistfully ; " won't you come upstairs and rest ? " " I would rather stair here ; you and I will have tea together, Helen, and talk over things. Of course," and she drew up her head proudly, "I know that Konneth is innocent. First he is simply incapnble of murder, next if in a moment of • madness he had injured anyone he would be the first to confess the truth; he is the very soul of honour; he is a Jardine you see, and our motto is truth." EvefS, word cut into Helen's heart like a sharp lash.: ever since the, moment of Alan- I dale's arts St she had suffered well-nigh a ! martyrdom of remorse; but perhaps her ! repentance had never been so real and acute as now, when ! the heiress sat beside her and tried to comfort her. • • She had done Magdalen- Jardine a bitter ,wrong in stealing the home and fortune which ! shoual have been hers front the moment that 1 the real Helen was drowned e she was nothing • ' but a miserable. impostor who had brought a ' load of sorrow mad ,disgrace upon a noble • house; little* wonder that her self-command gave way and she wejit Magdalen tried hard to comfort her. "You must not give up hope yet," she said tenderly ; -" indeed, indeed Alandale's innocence will be revealed at last. Even if no ray of light falls on the mystery before the trial at Ifamborough Assizes Hick. jury will be drawn from a More thoughtful intelligent • class than the men who 'gave the verdict at the inquest, and who thought it an act of duty to malign and belittle Kenneth just becanse he is an earl." linen lardine looked at Magdalen with an exprassio:i of wonder in her dark eyes. " How- geaal you are to me," she breathed. "I thought aiam would hate and despise Me." " Why ? " demanded the ether girl. "Surely youelnn't think I am so petty as to dislike you because you, happen to have a bettir claim to our grandfather's property than I lwave ? Shall I tell you somethina which will convince you of your mistake'? !ove Alandale dearly, but I never wanted to'! be the mistress of it ; if I had indeed come in for the estate I should have gone to some clever lawyer and asked him W 3 show me a way by which I could gives up everything to Kettle th." She spoke eagerly. With a certain simple energy that was more convincing than many ' potestations, and she did more than convince Wien of her indifference to riches: she be• 'rayed her own secret, that she loved Kenneth. Earl of Alandale, not as a cousin but with the one love of her woman's heart. Helen realised the link between them: she and Magdalen loved the sanrq man, the true heiress anti the false had bath given their beat affections to Kennetha How would it end ? He stood charged with a shameful crime, all Ids sufferings and humili- ations were, indirectly at least. Helen's fault. Magdalen had never brought him an hour's anxiety in her life, and yet the girl who had conic from over the sea to bring misery on an ancient name and honoured family would not have changed places with Magdalen for the world. Kenneth did not love Magdalen; in spite of her truth and courage, he only gave her a bzothe 4 affection, and deep down in Helen's

div.head: CHAPTER XIX.
div.p: CHAPTER XIX.

MAGDALEP. JARDINE 'and her cousin sat to- gether in the room which was known as Helen's boudoir one oppressive August day, when it wanted only a fortnight to Lord Alandale's trial. The two girls looked sadder and more cast down than at their first meeting, for the weeks which had passed had brought no lift- ing of the cloud hanging over Kenneth, and the two who loved him best on earth had strange misgivings that the truth about the murder, if discovered at all, would come to light too late tg save his life. "I feel as if I hated Sir John Leigh," said Helen bitterly; "he used to be one of Alan- dale's staunchest friends and. now he has gone over to the other side." "He couldn't," said Magdalen firmly; "he and Kenneth were school fellows and have been friends ever since; Sir John couldn'l think him guilty." "Well, anyway ke consorts with his enemies." said Helen. 'Sir John actually

Thornby Club, and when his aunt, the Daeht•,s of Quest, came to stay with him last week, she actually called at Rockmount and invited Miss Mackenzie to help at a bazaar she was getting up for some pet charity." "All the same, Helen, that does not prpve that John Leigh has taken sides against to- neth. As Mr. Mackenzie is one of the latter's most bitter foes, it looks to me more as though Sir John were trying to get on friendly terras with him so as to convert him."

"Then my discovery is worthless after all." "Not in the least ; all along Alandale's friends have been hampered by not being able to trace the weapon with which the murder was committed • the fact of its bearing the name of a MelbOuste firm proves it was /pur- chased in Australia ; can't you sketch in the rest of the details ? " " No," she shook her head, " I only thought of Miss Jardine." " Miss Jardine is a very beautiful woman.' said Sir John thoughtfully ; " it is almost im- possible to believe she had no lovers in her Colonial home. I should read the mystery like this, that one of them came over to Eng- land in search of .her, that coming to Thornbv he heard the rumours of Norton's pri% e meetings with the heiress of Alandale ani took the fellow's life in anger at the slur cast on his divinity." • Maria had listened with feverish eawcrneis. " Are you a 'lawyer ? All this' time I have been trying to think of some theory that would clear the Earl without condemning his cousin, and you find one at once." " Remember I am deeply intereetod in Alandale's fate," said Sir John, " and though not his lawyer, lam his friend. Now, will vou not trust me with your name that I may -see your father and persuade him to allow you -to give evidence in the Earl's favour.? " Maria looked horrified. "Pa will never consent," she said in a troubled tone, " and, Sir John, you prom%l me not to betralY me." " I will keep my promise," he assured her ; "but won't you tell me your name ? " "Maria Mackenzie. We live at .• Rock- mount and my father has set .his heart on seeing the Earl hung." she concluded naively. "Peter Mackenzie's daughter ! It seems impossible I "cried Sir John.

"It would be too late now," was Helen's answer ; " Sir John ought to know that. Mr. Mackenzie's malice was able to make things look blacker against Lord Alandale, but his good will, even if gained at the eleventh hour, could not break down the awful case of cur-. cumstantial evidence that has been raised igainst him. Magdalen, it is of no use fenc- ing with each other, we both know the truth in our hearts, Amnaate.s case is nopeless unless the true murderer is .discovered." "I have always thought so." admitted Magdalen. 'sand I have prayed night and day that Heaven would soften the real criminaL's heart and bring him to confession." "And your prayers arc answered, Mag- dalen,", Said Helen -sadly, "though in a sense you did not mean; I am going to give myselt up to the police to-morrow." "Helen, are you'mad ? Are you dreaming? What in the world makes you speak so rashly? I know perfectly you are as 'innocent of the , crime as Alandale himself, but if anyone else heard your rash words they might think that "That I spoke the truth. Weil, Magdalen, in a sense I do. If I had remained in Aus- tralia Norton or Blake, Ayhicliever you like to call him, would never have come here or lost , his life, so you sec, looking at the thing in one way, I.am his .murderer.'
Magdalen shivered. " You don't -know what you say," she ans- wered gently ; " trouble has driven you nearly wild."

Maria sighed. " Father made a fortune," she said frankly, "but he . was far happier before he ,iininlied making it. Now he is trying to get into society and it's harder work than getting ridt. Father used to be 'quite gobil-tonipered, • noir he simply hates everyone Who is of !liana rank than himself." - -

" I mean every word. Mr. Fielding is going to take me to see Alai:Atilt: this afternoon, anci —after that I shall give ,inys,Ai up." " You are not tit to go to tie prison.," saki Magdalen; " put it off till to-morrow," Helen shook Iter
" There is a report that lirinoth xvi!l be re- moved to Hamborough to-morrow, and I want to see him while he is still near us. And don't you see, Magdalen, that if the police 1312

when their friendship had first ripened, hut neither despairing nor terror-stricken, for Lord Alandale had managed to retain his frank open expression even in a prison cell. • He took both his cousin's hands in his and raised them reverently to his lips; his eyes brightened at the very E;ight of her, and yet the first words he 'addressed to her were a, re- proof." . " You should, not have come here, Helen ; it is no right place for you." " I came because I could not bear to stay away," she answered. " I wanted to see you badly. Oh,! Kenneth, do not say you areinot glad to sec me." " No face could be more welcome to me

than yours," he. said simply. " Helen, the time , for secrecy and concealment is over. Dearest. I must tell you the truth now. I -love you with all my heart and soul. I believe I loathsd that poor fellow of whose, death I at-n suspected iiist , because he had some private understanding With- you Had things gone differently with me the gulf between. our fortunes .might have kept me silent, but as it seems my days are numbered, as my friends believe I shall be called on to pay the penalty-of another's guilt, I mist speak frankly this once. • " I don't know when I began to love you, Helen ; 'I only know that you are my heart's desire, that I'd give the whole world just to call you mine." - • • " And I love you, she answered, "with all my heart and soul. Kenneth. I am the cause of your 4ouble and I will not let you suffer another day, I will wait no longer for the chance of the real murderer being found at the eleventh hour—to-morrow I shall give myself up ftfr the murder of Dick Blake." ` Dearest, are you mad ? " "No, I have been mad hitherto to let things • go so far, but that is over now. . Listen, Ken- neth, and you will see I am right ;- I know in my own heart I am the cause of your trouble and I have told you that .I love you.. Well, do you think that I could bear my life if I had to think of you as dead through my folly ? I have no one to regret me; Aunt Mary always looked a me as an intruder, she will fie happier far when the family honours 'devolve on Magdalen and poor Helen sleeps in a name- less grave." For all answer Lord Alanclale stretched out his arms and gathered Helen to his heart: . 1 " Dearest," he murmured pissionately, "do you think I could let you make such a sacri- fice for me ? Don't you know that my .life

would be worthless to me witnout you Helen, for my sake, for the love you say you bear me, promise to give up this 'dreadful scheme that has come into your mind." "I cannot, Kenneth; if you are condemned I should go out of my mind. I'd far rather die than face life without you. And," a choked sob broke her voice, indeed, indeed, life has not been such a happy 'thing to me that I should seek to cling to it. But in the end he had his way, for before they parted she had reluctantly given him the promise for which he pleaded. "If only fate would be kind to us," breathed Kenneth, as he pressed he ,to his heart, "how happy we might be. I am a proud man, Helen ; I used to think I could not bear to owe anything to my wisp, but now I feel I should not mind whether Alandale were yours or mine, so that you yourself were my own darling wife."
She looked into his 'face with her sweet sad eyes:„, _ _
"You love me," she whispered, "and few have loved me, but you think me good, Ken- neth; I am not good, I'm only a ' sinner, a woman who sorely tried has yielded to a terrible temptation.
"You are a woman," he answered fondly, "a woman, not an angel an angel is made to be reverenced, Helen, but a woman to be loved,"

He kissed her passionately on her lips, and as she yielded herself for one moment to the delight of. that caress, it seeemed to the poor troubled girl that she had never known what bliss meant before. If she had sinned sorely, she had as sorely suffered. Oh! why would not Heaven be merciful and let her die with that kiss upon her lips and Kenneth's arms about her?

div.head: WIDOW'S PATHETIC STORY. How She Survived a Terrible Struggle.
div.p: WIDOW'S PATHETIC STORY. How She Survived a Terrible Struggle.

"When my husband died, somewhat suddenly, leaving me with five little children, I had a terrible struggle to bring them up," said Mrs. Emma Jane Samplin, of Five Lanes, Caerwent, to a "Weekly Advertiser " representa- tive when relating how Bile Beans had proved a true friend in need to her. " flardl work and worry under- mined my health, and for several years I was a martyr to pain. "At first I used to have frequent headaches, then between my shOulders and around my heart I had most excruciating pains. Constipation and piles also caused me much suffering. Gradually my appetite failed,until I quite loathed the sight of food, and for a long time lived on liquids. I bad medical advice, and from time to time tried various remedies, but without deriving any lasting benefit. I was almost afraid to walk out- side the house alone for fear of falling down through dizziness, and as time went on I became so ill I was unable to stand or even dress myself, and had to be waited on hand and foot. 111'v hands and arms were numb and useless, and at last I was compelled to take- to bed. Then erysipelas broke out, and I was in a rash from head to foot. I really thought then I could not possibly survive. "About this time one of my sons advised me to try Bile Beans, and after taking a few doses the constipa- tion and piles were relieved. I followed uP the treat- ment, and the erysipelas soon left me. My skin is now as clear as that of a new-born babe. My hands and arms gradually lost their numbness, and I was able to leave my bed. My appetite also improved, and I can now go about my household duties cheerfully. I can with t‘onfidence recommend Bile Beans to all who suffer as I did." There is no finer household medicine than Bile Beans. They are gentle and genial in their action, and, unlike cheap substi butes and ordinary physic, Bile Beans can always be depended upon. A box is Is. ; large family size 2s. 9d.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.
The Examiner, Saturday, March 17, 1906. WOMAN'S REALM.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
A NEW FASHION.

The latest fad in table decoration is to com- pletely cover the cloth with blossoms. The flowers are spread in a close mass over the entire centre of the table, leaving only enough space for the necessities of the service. From the midst of the blossoms silver or rare china ornaments rise with charming effect. At a dinner recently given by the Princess de Broglie the table was hidden under a mass of pale roses; azalea blossoms and antique Dresden china were wonderfully effective on such a setting. Another dinner given by the Duchesse de In. Rochefoucauld had the cloth spread with Parma violets.

div.head: COSTTIME FOE THE SEASOE.
div.p: COSTTIME FOE THE SEASOE.

Our sketch chews a spring costume that is being realised in a bluish-heliotrope cloth, and is intended to be worn at an April wedding. The little coatee has collar and revers of velvet 4.q much deeper shade', and little points, faced with the same velvet, appear below the rounded fronts of the coat. The cape-like sleeves fasten over on top. and here again we find an inset of the dark velvet. The waistcoat fits very tightly, and is buttoned with minute velvet-covered but- tons The lace blouse which is worn underneath the coat is ef a very deep biscuit tint, and strap-

pings of cloti velvet appear on the cuffs. Once more skirts may fit tightly round the hips, and this dictum of fashion brings joy to many possessors of trim but short and plump figures, while the fact that they must be cut quite long, and very full round the hem, causes jubilation in the hearts of those long-suffering victims of fashion who have been striving to look slim and elegant in skirts that were the same width all the way down, and cut after the abbreviated fashion of the American trottoir. The chapeau that accompanies this costume is of horsehair exactly matching the cloth in shade; it is trimmed with small loops of ribbon in front, and is banked up at the back with a cache-peigne of hydrangeas.

div.head: GOSSIP.
div.p: GOSSIP.

In Paris, Gainsborough hats are to be seen, with many ostrich feathers. -These, when not ex- aggerated, are very picturesque. Most of the spring hats, however, are small, with trimmings of ribbon, or flowers underneath the brim, on one side or at the back. For such hats the hair must be dressed at the top of the head.

div.head: WHO WOULD NOT BE A DUCHESS?
div.p: WHO WOULD NOT BE A DUCHESS?

It is a great thing to be a Duchess, for a Duchess may do and dare things which would make a lesser being turn cold even to think of. At the ball given by the Duke and Duchess of Norfolk the other day, the Duchess wore the dress she was married in two years ago, and the "damaging" fact was duly chronicled by that section of the Press which deals with these things. Her Grace must be a brave woman, re- marks the Taller, for few society women would care to have widely published the fact that they wore at a big ball a two-year-old frock (their poor husbands, would they ever hear the last of it?), though the Duchess, who, as the Hon. Gwendo- len Constable-Maxwell, dressed in the simplest manner possible, is well known to care as little as her husband for sartorial. joys.

div.head: USEFUL MORNING FROCK.
div.p: USEFUL MORNING FROCK.

At this time of the year a neat, smart, and useful morning ft-0k is a valuable possession, particularly to the business woman. Just such a frock is pictured in our illustration. The mate- rial of which it is fashioned is A fine blue serge, light in weight and supple in weave. The bodice has a suggestion of the pretty pinafore style in its design, the shaped piece in front being re- peated at the back, the two meeting on the shoulders, where they are secured by large handsome buttons. The fulness of the bodice it

gathered on to this pinafore frpnt, and is drawn in at the waist by a belt of Soft blue kid, over which it is allowed to pouch slightly. In the the pinafore front appears a dainty lingerie chemisette of tucked lawn, finished with a turn-down collar and smart blue tie. This chemisette is, of course, detachable for laundry purposes. The skirt is perfectly plain, save for a panel front and a line of stitching at the hem, and is cut of serviceaille walking length. LADY BATTERSEA AND HER WORK.

The family of Rothschild has a double claim to .distinction, for it is famed for its finance and philanthropy. The immense wealth of this house is proverbial, but it is no less noted, says the Young Woman, for the kindly interest it takes in the poor of the "land. Lady Battersea, who is a Rothschild, and cousin of the present British head of the great banking house, married some thirty years back Mr. Cyril Flower, now Lord Battersea, said to be one of the handsomest men in London. She does a great deal for women of tho poorer classes, and would like to have social institutes for them 'in every village in England. Lady Battersea, until quite lale)y: used to hold a weekly class for Jewish scmpstresses, After the coronation, -Lady Battersea, like other Peeresses, made a profit, for charitable purposes, from the e4hibition of her ooronation tiara and robes.

WIDNES YOUTH'S SUICIDE. On Sunday afternoon a youth named Henry Edward Smith, aged seventeen, son of Henry Smith, 51, Wright-street, Widnes, committed suicide by hanging. Deceased went upstairs, and as he was a long time away his father sent one of the children to see where he was. The child reported that there was something tho matter with his brother, and on the father going into one of the bedrooms he found the deceased banging by two handkerchiefs to the bedsteads. Dr. Hutchinson was sent for immediately, but he pronounced life to be extinct. Deceasedhad been is good health.

div.p: NORTHERN ONION FIXTURES.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
Will of the Late Mr. H. B. White
-- The will of the late Mr. Henry Br3wn White, formerly maaistrates' clerk, of Warrington, has been proved at £2,133.

Popular Penny Concerts. A large audience assembled at the pipular penny concert in the Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom on Saturday evening, when an admirable programme was submitted. Songs were interpreted in a pleasing manner by thu Misses Dunn and lisy Isherwood. and Messrs. Gough, Jennings, Clayton, and Griffiths. Pianoforte solos were ably given by Mrs. B. Foreman, and Mr. A. Maybury caused much laughter with his sketches. The accompanist was Mrs. B. Foreman. A very enjoyable evening was spent. PIITILTC BENEFIT.—IINDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN T. 4 ANC IS Ti E. —Advt.

Engagement of Miss Sylvia Stanley. An event which is exciting great interest in Cheshire and North Wales is the forthcoming marriage of the Hon. Miss Sylvia Stanlev, second daughter of Lord and Lady Stanley of Alaerley, to the Hon. Anthony Henley, which has been arranged to take place in April, at Alderley. The charm of the ceremony will be considerably heightened bv the part which will be taken by the local school children, in whom Lord and Lady Stanley have taken a deep interest, and who are being specially trained for their part in the happy event.
J, R. Woon, Piano Dealer and Tuner,Friars Gate, and 47, Old London-road., Stockton Heath.--Advt. Certificated Class Teachers' Association.

A meeting of the above Association was held in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall on Saturday. There was a large attendance over which Mr. F. .1. Ernann presided. Mr. S. W. Jeffery (secretary) and the Chairman gave their reports of the gmeral aneeting of the Lancashire Federation of Assistant Teacher's' Association, which was held in Manchester on February 24th, and which they had attended RS delegates. It was decided to affiliate the local Association with the Lancashire Federation. A long discnssion ensued on the question of the " half-yearly reports, upon the conduct and work of assistant teachers," which are now required by the Education Committee from the head teachers. This new regulation has given rise to considerable dissatisfaction and unrest amongst local class teachers. and a proposition embodying a vigorous protest and defining a line of action was approved.
UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BooTs.—Ndvt.
Oddfellows' Social.

I The members of the " Loyal Friendship " Lodge o Odd fellows had a tea and social at the Blue Lion Inn, Market-place, on Saturday, to celebrate the 21st anniversary of the lodge. The proceedings which followed the tea were presided over by P.P.G.M. Henry Lengshaw, P.P.G.M. Thomas Knight was in the vice- chair, they being respectively first and second on the books of the lodge. The Chairman in proposing "The Friendship Lodge," said he was pleased to meet so many on the coming of age of the lodge, and he hoped it would go on prospering in the future as it had done in the past. Bro. Bramlsall responded. Bro. Knight, ,in responding for the Warrington District, said when ho became a member of the " Friendship" Lodge, 21 years ago, they had no district funds, but each lodge, ' was levied when a death occurred. He was happy to say they had now a district fund amounting to £5OO. Since the order was founded in Warrington each member had always received his full sick pay, as promised' when he joined his lodge. During the evening songs were rendered by Bros. Daniels, Green, Meacham, Litton, Dickinson, Burrress;and Pennington, jun. Bros, Pennington and Daniels were the accom- panists.
ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH...CLASS MINKRAL WATSRS.—Advt. P.S.A. Meetings.

There was a very large gathering of members and friends at the tsuckley-street P.S.A. meeting when the lhalf yearly distribution of prizes took place. Mr. B. ,IFew presided. The soloist was Miss Jenny Jones (St. IHelens) whose sweet sabrano voice was heard to great advantage in the solos " I know that my Redeemer liveth " and " Angels ever bright and fair." Miss M. Plinston was the accompanist. At the close of the meeting Alderman John Roberts distributed about 200 prizes to the members. Mr. Woolley and Mr. W. Hewitt also took part in the service.—The monthly open meeting of the Warrington Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Sunday, when Mr. E. Wynne Jones presided over an excellent attend- ance and in the course of a short address on " the necessity of a definite purpose in life " he stated that ,no life was complete without a purpose, and no man could be satisfied unless he had something to live for and it was only by spending our lives in loyalty to Jesus Christ that we could ever realize life's noblest purpose. Mr. C. M. Clarke delivered an address on " Sacrifice." Mr. B. Wadsworth's juvenile choir rendered two selections in a very creditable manner "-Stars that on your wondrous way " and' 0 taste and see." A. solo was also rendered by Miss Sarah Silcock. Councillor Clegg read the Scripture lesson.

LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SIIOES, UNDER THE CLOCK.BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt. Spiritualist Anniversary. The ninth anniversary of the Warrington Spiritualist Society was celebrated on Sunday by the holding cf special services. The speaker was Mr. W. Johnson, of Hyde, who, in the afternoon spoke of some of his " experiences with the so-called dead," which proved exceedingly interesting. He related how he had lapsed from Methodism into Atheism, from which he was rescued by coming into touch with Spiritualism. In the evening the subject was "Spiritualism and its tendencies." These briefly summed up were liberties of thought, freedom from doubt and dread of death, equality of opportunities for all, and fraternity of mankind, realizing that all were children of one Father. An augmented choir rendered the anthem "The Lord's Prayer," Mr. Fester presiding at the organ/ On Monday evening a public tea was held, followed by a social. Mr. R. Lee's instru- mental party rendered with considerable ability two marches, " The Goddess of War" and " Constella- tion." Mrs. Hannan sang " Flight of ages " and ' " Alannah " with taste, and, though suffering from a cold, was well received. Mr. Sidney Dark's violin solo, " The old folks at home," with variations, was loudly applauded. The President exhihted some speci- mens of direct spirit writing on slates, formerly the property of and obtained in the presence of the late Mr. Pemberton ; also a number of spirit photographs and some singular photographic results secured in an absolutely dark room, explaining the circumstances under which they were obtained. Miss Burke and Mr. Lee officiated at the piano. Games which_ were engaged in by the juniors and a number of selec tions on the phonograph,contributed to a very pleasant evening.

div.head: PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER TRE CLOCK. FOR BEST 1300 TS xw LANCASTICRE.—Advt. Children's Concert at the Parr Hall.
div.p: PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER TRE CLOCK. FOR BEST 1300 TS xw LANCASTICRE.—Advt. Children's Concert at the Parr Hall.

There was a large attendance at the Parr Hall on ' Monday evening on the occasion of a concert given by i Mr. T. Brough's jvvenile choir. An unusually capable combination the choir has established a high reputa- tion but this was the first occasion on which they ventured upon an entertainment in the Parr Hall with- out the assistance of senior t artistes. The results justified the ambitious step the proceedings being unusually successful. The programme opened with " The Village Blacksmith " sung by the choir, who number about Q. Well balanced the voices blended admirably, the children showed that. they had been subjected to caret ii training and I sang in a manner which reflected the greatest credit upon Mr. T. Brough. For their singing of "Merry little fellows" they were re-called twice "Kentucky home" was sweetly sung by Miss F. Bennett, who alsN joined Master W. Barlow in the duet "Eileen Alannah," the item being heartily encored. Miss E. Dunn and Master Barlow met with equal success in " When we are married." An act-ion song was prettily given by the Misses P. Barton and A. Brough, and was encored. A similar tribute of praise was paid to a mired party in the selection " Tell me, pretty maiden," the dancers being trained by Miss Ethel Spinks. Miss E. Vann and Master T. Tanner sang with effect "Barney. take me home again." whilst later in the evening Master Tanner joined Miss E. Dunn in the sucmsful item "Gipsy Countess." Miss Edith Jones and Master H. Bennett contributed " Killarney " and an Irish dance, the audience being so pleased with their efforts that the dance had to be twice repeated. " Your future husband" sung by half-a,dozen girls and boys was also heartily encored. Master J. Nurse, the butt-tourist of the choir created much amusement with his songs and for each item he had to make a second appearance. During the interval -a selection was contributed by the Legh-street Brass Band, under whose auspices the concert was held. Miss L. Horrabin was an efficient accompanist.

"When my little boy was three months old his head broke out with a rash, which was very itchy and ran considerable watery fluid. We triad everything we could, but he got worse all the time till it spread to his arms, legs, and then to his entire body, and he came near dying. It itched so he would scratch till the blood ran, and a thin yellowish stuff would be all over his pillow in the morning. I had to put mittens on his hands to keep him from tearing his skin. He got so weak he took fainting spells and we would think him dying. He was almost a skel. eton and his little hands were thin like claws. •

"He was bad about eight months when we tried Cuticura. I had not laid him down in his cradle in the daytime for a long time. He had got so that he just slept in our arms all the time. "I washed him with Cuticura Soap and put on one application of Cuticura Ointment and he was so soothed that I put him in the cradle. You don't know how glad I felt when he felt better. It took one box of Cuticura Ointment, pretty near one cake of Cuticura Soap, and. about half a bottle of Cuticura Resolvent, to cure. I think he would have died only for the Cuticura." MRS. M. C. div.head: MARCH 17th 1906.
div.p: MARCH 17th 1906.

Mr. GEORGE WYNDHAM did THE FISCAL not quite succeeci in talking DEBATE. out his own amendment on Tuesday. His eloquence had not enough staying power. He may, however, have found some compensation in the fact that he made Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN late for the dinner which be was giving to some political friends. This may be regarded as the sum total of the Conservative achievement in the somewhat prolonged debate initiated by Sir ;AMES Kirsox's motion, affirming, in effect, that the country has definitely and decisively expressed its mind on the subject of Free Trade. The Government majori- ties grew larger on each division, culminating in what must be the largest preponderance of votes on one side that has been known, where the party Whips were tellers, since Parliament began to assume its present constitution. Protectionism is, indeed, in this Parliament, dead and done for. DISRAELI, we remember, used a stronger phrase, for the proper expression of which the printer usually brings a long dash into play, But Protectionism we must admit, after all, is never wholly dead. It hibernates, emerging from its retirement at what are becoming fixed periods. It has, then, to be mere strictly accurate, been driven to its earth, owing nothing, we venture to think, to the gentleman who made the last stand on its behalf.

A more wandering, aimless, and feeble dis- cursiveness than has distinguished the speeches from the Unionist Benches of the House of Commons during the first two days of this week there could not be. One speaker after another betrayed an extraordinary anxiety to discourse on anything but Free Trade, and had to be called up more or less peremptorily by Mr. LowTrom for irrelance. When members of the opposition did endeavour to confine themselves to the matter in hand, they made the most astound- ing revelation of their unfamiliarity with the facts which govern the consideration of the subject, and with the varied experiences ad national benefits on which the present belief .in Free Trade is grounded. Politicians like Mr. GEORGE Wricn- HAM seem never to have given any attention to the economic aspect of the question until they. were compelled to do so by way of defending Mr. CnAatnEnnAtx. Then they were like Keats's " Watcher of the Skye," who sees some new• planet swim into his ken, or rather they were like a schoolboy who has no sooner come into possession of a toy telescope than he begins to make astronomical discoveries, in which he ,I was anticipated from some hundreds to some thousands of years ago. Mr. WYNDHAM told the House of Commons that he and his friends claim to he believed when they say that they are not considering questions of party advantage, but that they are concerned about national trade, and that they are desirous of drawing the Empire more closely together. Well, if they have it so, we have no objection to make the concession. We will not insist on pointing out that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN did not think of these things until he was con- fronted with the vastness of his South African failure. We shall merely take the liberty of sug- gesting that if Mr. WYNDHAM and his friends are so deeply concerned about the national trade they should have made themselves more familiar with the conditions under which it is carried on,and that if they desire to draw the Empire more closely together they should not awaken ,disaffection and disgust by suggesting that our Colonies will desert the Mother Country if they are not bribed to remain with us. There is, even on the Liberal side, some feeling that the time taken up by Sir JAMEs KirsoN's resolution has been thrown away. In one sense it has, of course,but the adoption of the resolution by so tremendous a majority has saved much future time, and has, besides, per- formed the inestimable service of showing that the question on which gentlemen on the Conservative benches desire most to carry the country with them, is precisely that question on which they are the most ill-informed and muddle•headed.

It is amazing what spleen TREE-PLANTING and bitterness have arisen AMENITIES. from the "Beautiful Stockton Heath " move- ment. The tree planting scheme may make a verdant paradise of the village some day, but at the present time it seems to have been responsible for sowing the seed of sectional discord with every tree—and the seed is flourishing better than the trees. Many people think the ardent tree-planters have overdone their part, and the evidence in favour of this view seems incontestable. But the tree planters will not admit it, and they are annoyed that the District Council differs from them, and has appointed the Highways Committps to visit the village and see for itself. On Thursday evening, the Parochial Committee repudiated Mr.
A
kliW4
3 I

Whitley. That gentleman stood virtually with his back to the wall while the Committee barked at him. We support Mr. Whitley in this matter, and we are glad to see that he did not flinch from the unpleasant ordeal of attending a meeting where he knew every hand and voice would be against him. He was perfectly right to represent to the District Council the views of those people who considered the trees a nusisance and a danger in many places where they have been planted. Possibly he spoke for the minority, but Mr. Clarke should remember that in these days minorities are entitled to be heard even if majorities role- The fact cannot be gainsaid that many of the trees are planted on footpaths where there is no room for them, with the result that pedestrians—even members of the Parochial Committee—have to walk in the road when they, go abroad with their umbrellas and wives. Utility should not be sacrificed to appear- ances, and if the footpaths would look very nice covered with trees that is no reason why a Con- scientious Councillor like Mr. Whitley should not point out to the authorities that the footpaths were primarily intended to be walked on. We hope he will persist in his action until the tree-planting scheme is brought within reasonable bounds.

There is little need to POOR CIIILDREN'S emphasise the benefit which CAMP. • hundreds of Warrington children have derived from that most recent of beneficent undertakings—the Poor Children's Summer Camp. The dwellers in some of the poorest parts of the town are enabled to spend a delightful holiday amidst the picturesque surroundings of Prestatyn and return looking the pictures of health and vip,•our. We are pleased to hear that several new departures—which many will highly appreciate—are contemplated. In the first place the camping ground and foreshore at Prestatyn have been leased from Lady McLaren for fourteen years, and efforts are being put forth to establish the camp on a more prominent basis. An Assembly Room is about to be built and will prove a great boon for recreative and other useful purposes. It is also proposed to erect wooden huts or cubicles for use in place of tents—an advantage which is obvious when one considers the vagaries of the climate. An innovation which will be of even greater interest to the general public is that during the time the camp is unoccupied by the children it is hoped to hire the huts at a small charge to people whose circumstances would not permit of the expense of an ordinary seaside holiday and especially to convalescents. The concession will, we are sure, be heartily welcomed and the camp will thus serve a double advantage to Warrington. There will, of course, be an additional claim upon the generosity of the townspeople before the improvements are accomplished, hot we believe that the response to the appeal which will shortly be made will be sufficiently generous to extinguish the present deficit of £3l7s. 10d., and place the institution on a Founder basis to pursue an enlarged work.

We notice that in the TEE LABOUR PARTY debate on one of the amend- Arm FREE TRADE. ments to the Government's Free Trade resolution Mr. ter Hardie went out of his way to explain that Labour members " were not committing them- to the theory that Free Trade was the issue 'lcon which they won the election." This repudi- ation of the great free food question is ungenerous c,r`n the part of Mr. Kier Hardie and his followers. ?ay what they will, the fact remains that very "alw of them would have been successful but for the fact that the workers all over the land were up in arms against the proposal to combat tariffs by raising the cost of food. If the Labour members had not openly and actively espoused Free Trade and free food they would have been "left " on the day of election and Mr. Hardie knows this as Well as anyone else. It may suit Labour to imagine that the victories were the triumphs of Lebow as Labour pure and simple, but the fact remains that Labour is indebted to the great national upheaval caused by the introduction of fiscal heresies and the employment of Chinese Labour. We heartily admit that Labour has made great strides as a political force—and we welcome the intelligent advance of the democracy—but uld d this ePrecate too exalted an attitude over the next atcroungsgicli:rable electoral triumph. When rd inda very h comes, Labour will have to fight at (led to maintain the position now held, A will need all the extraneous help it can get from those party cries which happen to be to the fore at the moment. Mr. Hardie and his friends floated buoyantly in on the Free Trade tide, and they will have to beware of the ebb.

Members of the defeated " Tuarrixa OFF party at the General Elec. THE TAP." tion have, of late, professed great jubilation at the fact that the Government has not stopped the employ- ment of Chinese slave-labour. Some of them have even gone so far as to say that members of the Government were pledged to end it summarily on Corning into power. Reasonable people, however, are well satisfied with the course of affairs up-to- date. The first thing the new Government did ,was to stop the issue of new licences for Chinese labour,so that there would be n o further importation' of the Chinamen except under existing contracts. r.uch has been made of the fact that the Govern • -aent is allowing some 16,000 Chinamen to enter the Transvaal over and above the number ern- Pleyed whew the last government went out of office. The Goverment was helpless in the matter, unless it took the extreme and costly step of breaking the contracts which were in existence and compensating the contractors. During the Closing days of the old regime the mine-owners., With what Mr. Churchill calls " an intelligent 1 anticipation of events,'" took out thesel 16,000 licenses, which it will take till Julyl to work off. From that date it may be taken for granted that no more Chinaman will be I admitted to the Colony except as free men and with the rights of citizenship. On Wednesday,l in the House of Commons, Mr. Churchill made a very important announcement which justifies this assumption. In regard to the supply of Chinese, he said : "The Imperial Government proposed to instruct the consular officers to resume the authority which they had delegated to the agents, and not to exercise it themselves. This " .remarked Mr. Churchill amid loud cheers, "would ~ ~'".„.ciro the tap off." It will not ruin the mines. " e do not believe that the cheap Chinaman is the basis of the mining industry. He was not neces- a.ery to it before the war ; he was not necessary to it afbr the war, when the mineowners acted deliberately with a view to checking the supply of black labour and to destroying the possibility of White labour. He is not necessary at all, and it is the bounden duty of the G -worriment of this eountry,'at the earliest opportunity, to put an end to the iniquitous system of slavery instituted in order to satisfy the rapacity of the Raadlords.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 17, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 17, 1906.
The Liberal Association.

The annual meetings of the General Council and Executive Committee of the Warrington Liberal Association will be held this (Friday) evening at 7.30 at the Liberal Club. Officers for the ensuing year will be elected and other business discussed. Notice.

The Warrington "Examiner" is now published on Friday afternoon, price one penny, and is on sale at the various newsagents at about 4 o'clock. Should any difficulty be experienced in getting the paper the proprietors will undertake to deliver a copy at any address in Warrington by 5 o'clock on Friday after- noon without'extra charge. Address all communica, tions to" Examiner Office," Bewsey-street Warrington Suicide Follows Dismissal. Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the body of James Henry Bradshaw, a compositor, of MO, Church-place, Warnngton, which was recovered from the Mersey on Tuesday morning. The evidence showed that the deceased was, up to a short time ago, employed with a Manchester firm of printers, but owing to slackness of work he was discharged. The dismissal, after twenty-five years' service, seemed to prey on his mind, and on Tuesday last he left his lodgings, and did not return. A verdict of " Found drowned " was returned. THE CYCLE of EASE is the "Premier." Prices, 7, 8, 10, 12, and 14 guinens.—Fall stock at J. S. GARLAND'S showrooms, 51, 53, & 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Choir Social and Presentation. The trustees of the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church on Wednesdey evening invited the members and friends of the choir to a grand social, with a view to making a presentation to their respected choir- master and organist. During the evening congratu- latory speeches were made by the officials of the Church, who spoke in eulogistic terms of the services rendered in the past by these gentlemen. The speakers were the Rev. C. L. Stowe, Mr. J. Bissell, Mr. J. G-riffiths and Mr. B. T. Parkes, and suitable responses were made by the choirmaster (Mr. A. Spruce) and Mr. F. Poduaore. Quartettes and solos were rendered by members and friends of the choir, and altogether a most enjoyable evening was spent. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt.

Colonel Pilkington and his Defeat. The annual meeting of the Warrington Polling District of the Newton Division Conservative Associa- tion was held in the Schoolroom, Padgaite, on Tuesday evening, Alderman Francomb presiding.—The Chair- man said he was sorry they did not win the election. (Hear, hear.) It was a cruel thing to lose such an excellent member, and to get such a poor spicimen in his place. He knew who was the best friend, both to rich and poor, and that was Colonel Pilkington. It was astonishing why such a revolutionary change should take place. —Colonel Pilkington returned thanks to all who had voted for him and assisted him during the last election. He believed that he had lost his seat through the cry of Chinese Labour more than any- thing else, and there were never such, shameful mis- statements made. So far tho performances of the Liberal members in Parliament had been ridiculous and absurd, and instead of saving money, they had been spending it on themselves. They had actually passed a resolution t fill their own pockets with salaries. Let them stand by the party that wished to keep this country together, .to give them good laws, which had taken hundreds of years to make. He would make any sacrifice rather than see the old flag go down. (Applause.)—The following officers were elected : Alderman Francomb (chairman), Mr. George Mather and Mr. William Houghton (vice-chairmen), Alderman Bennett, Mr. William Houghton and Mr. William Fryar (delegates to the Council).

Fatal Accident at Warrington. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Warrington Police Station on Wednesday, on the body of George Caldwell, aged 38, carter, of 31, James- street, Widnes, who received fatal injuries on Satur- day whilst discharging a load of corn at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' stables in Dallam-lane, War- rington. Samuel Taylor, 129, Dallam-lane, a carter in the employ of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, said on Saturday last deceased brought a load of corn from Messrs. Fairclough's corn mills. Deceased was engaged on the furry adjusting the chain round the neck of the sacks so that they could be hoisted into the loft. Witness was in the loft receiv- ing the sacks. Whilst hoisting one of tho sacks the chain slipped from off the neck just as witness was receiving it. The mishap caused him to overbalance, land he fell from the loft, a distance of twelve feet, on 'to the lurry, being rendered unconscious. Deceased was knocked off the lurry on to the ground. Joseph Bate, a carter in the employ of Messrs. Fairclough and Sons, said a hook was used at the end of the chain instead of a ring. Just before the accident he heard someone say "Hold on a minute mate. Pat the chain round the 'lug' of the bag instead of in the middle." In reply to Mr. Lewis,his Majesty's Inspector of factories witness stated that a ring was much safer than hook. —Mr. Brighouse said the jury were not called upon to checide whether it was safer to use a hook or ring. Those enquiries were made fishing ponds for the legal gentlemen who got as much information as they could to enable them to thrash out their legal responsi- bilities. The duty of the jury was to find whether death was due to accident or not.—. verdict of " Accidental death " was returned, and the jury expressed the opinion that a ring was more favourable for a hoist.--At the inquest Messrs. Pearson and Knowles were represented by Mr. F. S. Taylor, Mr. Unsworth appearing for the relatives of deceased and Messrs. Fairclough and Sons. Concert In the Parr Hall

An enjoyable concert was held in the Parr Hall on Tuesday, the proceeds of which werb in aid of the St. Mary's (R.C.) Working Girls' Club. There was a large attendance and the funds ,of the Club—a thoroughly deserving institution—should materially benefit as the result of the venture. An excellent programme was opened by Mrs. John Dolan, who sang with effect " Down the Vale." The possessor of a sweet voice, she later in the evening met with equal success in "The castle builders," being very warmly applauded. Mr- J. Rabbitt was admirably suited ia "Lend me your aid " (Gounod) composition affording ample scope for dramatic effect to which the singer did full justice, his soulful rendering charming his hearers. In " The Last Watch " (Ciro Pottutt) he was beard to equal advantage. " Hejre Kati " rebav) as played by Mr. R. H. Pearscn left little to be desired, ,1 and the artiste was called upon for a second 1 contribution. His other items "Melody in B fiat" (Benotti) and " Bolero " (Irubag) were given in a manner which\ was equally pleasing. The principial vocalist of the evening was Nfiss Marie Houghton wlto was accorded a very warm reception. As she was suffering from a cold it was only after 'considerable hesitation that she consented to sing, but she gave such an artistic interpretation of " The Nightingale " that any disability which , she suffered from her temporary indisposition was hardly apparent. Her efforts were greeted with an enthusiastic outburst of applause. With Miss L. Fairhurst, Mr. Rabbitt and Mr. J. W. Bibby,she also took part in the quartette"The budding bloom of May" ( Wiivatz), which was given with such excellent effect as to call forth a hearty encore. Mr. T. W. Bibby could hardly have chosen a more accept- able song than "Three for Jack " (Squire) which, was given with a delightful swing and earned for him a hearty encore. Miss L. Fairhurst was heard to advan- tage in " Killarney" but perhaps the audience were more pleased with the pretty song which she gave in response to a recall. She was also very warmly applauded for the song " Come back to me" which she accorded sympathetic treatment. Miss Sexton very ably rendered Mascheroni's "Till death " for which she was well received. The League of the Cross brass quartette rendered " Bach's fugue in G Minor" (arranged by Mr. F. Podmore) in a very capable manner. Little iault could be found with their play- iag but it would have been better had they cho.tea a composition with which the audience could have been in greater sympathy. Mr. Matt de Lacey aroused considerable amusement with his Irish sketches. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., ably discharged the duties of accompanist.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. --- ALLEGED RUNCORN BURGL tRY.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. --- ALLEGED RUNCORN BURGL tRY.

About midnight on Tuesday a Runcorn constable, at the police station, heard a sound of breaking glass, and going across the street, he found a man with his hand through the shop window of Tereza Leigh, directly opposite the police office. He had taken cigars, cigarettes, and other articles. The man proved to he a stranger named Thomas Brown. On Wednesday the magistrates remanded him for inquiries. WIDNES COMPANY'S NEW WORKS AT NEWCASTLE. A Newcastle telegram says :—lt was stated at the annual meeting of the Newcastle Electric Supply Com- pany that the Castner-Kelner Chemical Company, of Widnes, would shortly establish works on the Tyne, and take from the company 13,000,000 units a year, working night and day, Sundays included.

RUNCORN URBAN COUNCIL ELECTION. The annual election of representatives on the Runcorn Urban Council takes place on the 31st inst. Nomina- tions must be at the office of the Returning Officer (Mr. F. A. Lake), 55, High-street, not later than noon on ThursdaYAthe 15th. Withdrawals may be made up to noon on Tuesday, the 20th. The retiring councillors are Messrs. S. Taylor (Halton Ward), J. J. Shaw (Mersey Ward), J. H. Salkeld (Central Ward), G. Hewitt (Bridgewater Ward), J. Wilson (Newtown Ward), and J. W. Lightburn, (Heath Ward). Mr. \V. Shaw, jun., will oppose Mr. Wilson in the Newtown Ward. Other names have been prominently mentioned in con- nection with Heath Ward, from the representation of which it is understood Mr. Lightburn is retiring, but nothing definite has yet been decided.

div.head: DEATH OF DEAN FINEGAN.
div.p: DEATH OF DEAN FINEGAN.

The death took place on Friday afternoon of the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, of St. Bede's Presbytery, Appleton, Widnes. The late Dean Finegan was born at Navan, in county Meath, in January, 1841, and was, 65 years of age, He received his education at Navan Seminary and afterwards at Lisbon. Ws first appointment as a priest was at St. Edward's College, and he afterwards pro- ceeded to St. Mary's, Barrow. In 1875 he came to St. Bede's, Appleton, and two years later he was made dean. On that occasion he was presented with a gold watch and purse of gold. in 1900 be was the recipient of an address and monstrance. The Dean was one of the most familiar figures in Widnes. His goodness of heart and his cheery disposition endeared him to all. The Dean took the liveliest interest in matters educational and was connected with the old School Board from November, 1877,until its absorption by the new author- ity,. He served on the district Education Committee, and the School Management Committee. He acted as chairman of the latter committee from 1880 to 1895. He was appointed a member of the Widnes Education Committee and School Management Sub-committee on June Ist 1903. The funeral took place on Tuesday at Widnes Cemetery in the presence of a large concourse of townspeople. RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB—ANNUAL MEETING. The annual general meeting of the members of the Runcorn Cycling Club was hold at the Brunner Guild Hall on Monday evening. Mr. F. Cringhall presided over a representative attendance.—The Hon. Secretary (Mr. W. Booth) reported that the club had had some little ups and downs but had closed the season with a membership of 68. The turn outs were not so satisfactory and he hoped, especially in regard to the Wednesday section, the new committee would endeavour to effect an improvement. The average turn out for the Saturday sectio9 was 29, and of the Wednesday section 11. The committee had decided to give three attendance medals to each section.—The Treasurer (Mr. G. A. Kirkham), presented the financial report. The year was com- menced with an adverse balance of £3 2s. Bid. and closed with a balance in hand of £2 15s. 3d. Special subscriptions were given by Sir John Brunner, Alder- man A. R.Norman, and Messrs. S. Taylor, F.J.Norman, , H. Congreve, R. H. Posnett, H. Turton, and J. Wilding. The report was adopted.—The election of officials , resulted as follows :—President (deferred) ; vice- presidents, Sir J. T. Brunner, Alderman Norman, and Messrs. F. J. Norman, R. Congreve, and R. H. Posnett ; hon. members, Dr. MacLennan, and Messrs. H. Turton, J. Wilding, J. J. Shaw, R. H. Pringle, A. Abel, H. Chadwick, J. M. Frith, G. Luxton and P. Hollinshead ; hors secretary, G. A. Kirkham; bon treasurers, W. IMack ; captain Wednesday section, J. Stanway ; sub- captain, R. Burman: captain Saturday section, J. Green; sub-captain, W. Asbbrooke ; committee, Messrs. Taylor, Hindley, Hedgecock, Prescott, Booth, Lightfoot, Millinger, Cringhall, and J. J. Charlesworth , delegates N.C.U., Messrs. Bankes and Gibbs ; auditors; Messrs. Powell and Holt ; representative on Guildhall Committee, Mr. Booth ; representative on the Cottage Hospital Committee, the Secretary. It was decided to present gold medals for attendance to the following at a social gathering:—K. Jennion, H. Smith and J. Stan. way (Wednesday section) ; J. Jackson, P. Smith, and J. Hedgecock (Saturday section).

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
AN ANCIENT PROFESSION.

I Thomas Croft, a painter, belonging to Southport, was described at St. Helens on Monday as a professional beggar.—The Chief Constable said that he saw Croft begging at the houses in Kiln-lane, opposite to his residence. He then came to his back door, and told the servant that he was a St. Helens man and had been in hospital. The Chief Constable then interviewed him and sent for a constable. Croft's pockets were stuffed with bread, and he had is. 31-d. in coppers. On the way to the Town Hall he told the constable he knew he was done for when he saw the Chief Constable.—Croft argued the matter out with the bench for some time, until his character from a former employer was read, when he was sent to gaol for twenty-eight days hard labour. ST. HELENS AND RELIGIOUS EDUCATION. A large and enthusiastic meeting of parents and others was held in St. Thomas's Church Schools, St. Helens, on Monday evening. The Rev. H. Gibson Smith, vicar of Allerton, was the speaker. He said that since parents were compelled by law to have their children educated, they had a right to demand that their children should be taught the faith they themselves I believed. The State could do a great many things, but it could not stifle the desire for God in the human heart, which desire expressed itself in the demand for definite religious education.
