div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Increasing traffic is adding to the complexities of Ship Canal navigation and in consequence a con- siderable number of masters and mates of vessels that use the Manchester Ship Canal are presenting to the managers of that great waterway a petition for its better lighting and signalling. * * Colonel Kenyon-Slaney, M.P., the Tory landlord member for the Newport Division of Salop, dis- tinguished himself in the House of Commons this week by sitting on his hat after concluding a vehement denunciation of the Liberal party. He was probably thinking of the party when he sat on the hat. We understand that the weight of his body did more damage than the weight of his denunciation. The tree-planters are still down on Mr. Whitley, and in a lengthy indictment of him on Thursday, Mr. Clarke said " Mr. Whitley, when he goes to Dutton, meets another class of gentlemen." It is interesting to know that there are two classes described as gentle- men in Stockton Heath and Dutton, but we are not informed which are " first " and which are " second " class. Presumably the male inhabitants of these two districts consist of "gentlemen—and others." A proper classification for census returns would be interesting. * * Several legal and medical gentlemen engaged in the " jam prosecution " at the Warrington Police Court 'on Tuesday spent a considerable time in trying to work out a simple decimal sum. It was in vain, for all the answers were different, and it had been almost decided to give up the attempt when the Borough Analyst came to the rescue and supplied the correct figures. Thus the situation was saved and some slight proof afforded that elementary education is of more importance than religious instruction in the day schools.

* * * An enthusiastic member of the Beautiful Warring- ton Society has a particular grievance against the smoke nuisance. He has in times past attempted to cultivate snowdrops in the region of Sankey street but thanks to our smoke-laden atmosphere, the flowers were almnst black before he was able to cut them ! The Society will indeed be doing a useful pervice if it induces manufacturers to adopt means to) avoid the present output of dense smoke. It is certainly one of the first steps—though perhaps a rather difficult one— by which the town can he made more pleasant and attractive. . .

* * Mr. Francis Neilson, who is well known to Warrington Liberals as a public speaker, has earned the gratitude of the Liberals of the Newport division of Shropshire for the plucky fight which he made at the recent general election against Colonel Kenyon- Slaney. On Wednesday these feelings found tangible expression in the presentation to Mr. Neilson of a gold watch and albert and illUminated address, to Mrs. Neilson of a tea and coffee serve, kettle, and spirit lamp, and a pair of massive candlesticks, all of solid silver';:to her young daughters, of gold necklets and lockets and ladies' bicycles.

* * * The vigilance of the public in watching their own affairs is undoubtedly bearing fruit, and the Corpora- tion is evidently getting more business-like. At the Local Government Board Inquiry on Wednesday into the borrowing of £7,000 for electrical purposes it was stated that none of the money had yet been spent, but was required for future developmets. It has been the fashion for the Corporation to " spend " the money and then to" apply ' for it. The practice has been described by the Mayor as " monkeying" with the Local Government Board, and since they found it did not pay the Corporation have discontinued it. Under close supervision they seem likely to develop quite a model character. There was an amusing • incident at the Beautiful Warrington meeting at Cairo-street schools on Tues- day evening. The hon. secretary related the story of agentleman who met him one day and while expres- sing profound admiration of the Society's aims, unthinkingly produced some papers from his pocket, began to tear them up and throw the fragments on the ground.Of course,the moral of the ancedote was.that that was not the way to make Warrington beautiful, and the meeting laughingly agreed. Later, however, they were somewhat surprised when a member rose and confessed that he was the culprit ! Another enthusiast—an alderman—told how he was about to commit a similar misdeed when be recalled the secretary's admonition and restored the paper to his pocket. * * * The Tories of Padgate have evidently taken their defeat at the general election with very bad grace, for at their meeting in Padgate Schools field last Tues- day, several of the speakers used most extraordinary language. The Chairman (Mr. Alderman Francomb) after making a statement that they would not " call " the present Member—then went on to say"lt was cruel to lose such an excellent Member as Colonel Pilking- ton and to get such a poor specimen in his place." If this is not calling" a Member we do not know what to" call" it. However, we may inform Alder- man Francomb and his friends that the Labour Party are proud of their new Member, Mr. Seddon, and are strongly of the impression that he will in his new sphere accomplish more good for the electorate than Colonel Pilkington * * * Another speaker at Padgate, Mr. Deacon, referring to the Education Act, said the " present arrangement suited the Roman Catholics, the Church of England, and all others except the small balance, the miser- able clique called Free Churchmen. " The language is, of course, more forcible than polite, and we may add that the Free Churchmen, instead of being a "small balance " of the nation, represent more than one half of it. We would suggest to our Tory friends that calling names and using insulting language is just the wrong way to win back a constituency, and that such tactics are sure to recoil upon them. * * *

The Ship Canal Action. Lord Justice Vaughan on Wednesday directed that the application to settle the minutes and motion as to costs in the recent action between the Warrington traders and the Ship Canal Company should be heard in the Court of Appeal on March 28th.

Coming Events. A lecture on " A Tour in the Highlands of Southern France " will be delivered by Mr. Hubert Congreve in the Bold-street schools, on Monday evening. Mr. James Dodds will preside. Mr. Congreve is well known to Warrington audiences as a lecturer whose addresses are unusually interesting, and a large audi- ence should welcome him on Monday evening. The lecture will be illustrated by limelight views from photographs taken by Mr. Congreve. TiO, programme at the popular penny concert to-night will be submitted by the Misses Hayes, Millard, Mounfield, Houghton, Parr, Osborne, Grounds, and Tonge, and Messrs. Hamilton, Baines and Isher- wood. The annual meeting of the Governors of the War- rington Infirmary will be held at the Town Hall on Thursday.

The Council and Bolin School. A special meeting of the Town Council will be held on Monday afternoon at four o'clock to consider the business contained in requisitions received by his Worship, viz., to rescind the confirmation of the minutes of the Town Council passed March 6th, 1900, referring to the proceedings of the Education Com- mittee in so far as those proceedings refer to the acceptance of the tender for building the Bolton School, and also those passed April 11th, 1905, referring to the acceptance of the competitive plans submitted by Messrs. Wright, Garnett and Wright.

Death of Mr. John Fieldhonse. We record with regret the death, which took place on Thursday morning at his residence, Hanover-street, of Mr. John Fieldhouse. Deceased, who celebrated his 80th birthday last week, had been in failing health ifor twelve months. He came to Warrington twenty-five years ago as works manager at Bewsey Forge, having for 2.5 years previously been manager for Messrs. G B. Thornicroft and Co., Wolverhampton. IA) retired, from business about 20 years ago. In politics he was 1 a staunch and active Liberal. He was one of the oldest members of the Baptist Church, Golborne- street, and was an elder of the Church, being held in very high respect by his fellow worshippers. A man of strong character, he leaves a large number of friends to mourn his loss. The funeral will take place this Saturday afternoon at Hill Cliffe: Seven Guineas will buy a "PREMIER " BICYCLE, . .

div.head: keep up:—Sole Agen;,.S:'S.dARLAND, 51, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Fire in a Cellar.
div.p: keep up:—Sole Agen;,.S:'S.dARLAND, 51, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Fire in a Cellar.

Shortly after noon on Thursday a flie broke out on the !premises of Mr. Wm. Parkinson, hay and straw dealer, Union-street. The fire brigade were summoned and turned out with remarkable promptitude being on the scene within a few minutes of the out- break being noticed. Under the command of Superin- tendent Turner a full complement of men at once commenced to fight the fire, the hay and straw in one of the cellars lacing well alight. It was only with extreme difficulty that the men were able to get to the seat of the fire on account of the intense heat and the dense volumes of smoke which issued from the cellar, and even with damp cloths over their mouths they had to be relieved every few minutes. The fire was quialy got under control and was finally extinguished after about two hours' work. The damage, which is considerable, is fully covered by insurance.

ASK for CIINNENIGILAM'S HIGFI-CLA.Sh MINBRA.T. WATERS.—Advt. Presentation at Messrs Houghton. Perhaps one of the best ways to sweeten life is that of cultivating an interest in the lives of other people,a pleasing instance of which took place at the wori.s of Messrs. Houghton's, Sankey Bridges. A week or two ago Mr. Highley celebrated his 70th birthday and the event suggested itself to his fellow workmen as an appropriate occasion on which to show in some smalk way their mark of esteem for him. So on Saturday' last Mr. Highley was presented by his fellow workmen with three beautiful books viz. :—" The Last King " by Di'. Beer, " President Roosevelt " and " The Traveller." Needless to say he was delighted with the gift and one and all wished him a continuance of that remarkable vitality which he happily possesses. Mr. Highley has worked for Messrs. Houghton for upwards of 30 years as a wiredrawer. BA.BY CARRIAGES. _New and Artistic designs.—

J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51:53, & 55, Bridge St., Warringtou.—Advt: Junior Liberal Meeting. There a good attendance at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association which was held at Gregory's Cafe on Monday. evening, when an excellent paper on "William Morris" was presented by Councillor Ball. Mr. E. Osborne presided and heartily congratulated Councillor Ball upon his election as a representative of St. John's Ward. Councillor Ball was a gentleman with high ideals and it was to be hoped that he would allow his ideals to have full play in the Town Council.—Councillor Ball dealt with his.subject in a very able and interesting manner. The subject of his address he said was a man of wide attainments and wide sympathies. As poet, artist, manufacturer, socialist and author William Morris was a remarkably gifted man. Having dealt with his earlier life he sketched the career of Morris as a writer of poetry and prose. As a manufacturer he had high ideals of the introduction of beauty into the homes of the people and as a designer of furniture, tapestry, &c., he endeavoured to carry out those ideals. The work aof Morris as a communist was also briefly touched upon. A brief discussion followed, the proceedings closing 'with a vote of thanks to Councillor Ball, accorded on the motion of Mr. Barlow seconded by Mr. Gray.

div.head: TREE PLANTING AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: TREE PLANTING AT STOCKTON HEATH.
LIVELY DISCUSSION AT THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.
fdr. Whitley Taken to Task.

The question of tree planting in Stockton Heath— one which of late has given rise to considerable dis- cussion—occasioned a debate at the monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee, of a some- what personal and heated character. The meeting was held at the Hall Cafe under the chairmanship of Mr. George Pilling. The discussion was opened by Mr. H. J. Westbrook who said he would like to make a personal explana- tion with regard to his remarks re the tree planting deputation. He saw that the District Council had I resolved " That this Council regrets that a member of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee should have gone out of his way to ieflect upon the District Council, in the way he has done, as such remarks are not conducive to the interests of the District Council and the Parochial Committee." His remarks were based, after careful inquiry, upon certain , remarks which were made at the District Council meeting. Some confusion seemed to exist as to whether the remarks were made by the Council, as I such, or individually so he fired two shots one of which seemed to have hit. He had no feeling I against the District Council but it seemed to him that such remarks as were made at the Council meeting ' were disturbing to the happy relations which hitherto existed between that body and the Parochial Com- mittee. Perhaps he expressed himself strongly but he felt strongly and was an entirely unconverted and unrepentant sinner. His remarks were based upon supposition and if the supposition was wrong he asked that his remarks should be treated as not applicable. For the time being the subject closed and some ordinary business was disposed of. At the end of the meeting Mr. J. H. Clarke said he desired to call the/attention of the Comittee to a speech delivered by one of their District Councillors at the last meeting of the Council. He desired td bring the matter before the committee as a protest that Mr. Whitley was misrepresenting the I committee when he went to Dutton. (Hear' hear.) I He was sorry to have to do so as Mr. Whitley had been a good member of the committee for some years and it , was not often that they took different views—(Mr. Whitley: "I am sorry that we do this time.")—and he, regretted very much that he had to raise the question ' that night. Mr. Whitley: Mr. Chairman is this in order ? Mr. Pilling: Yes. Mr. Clarke (in a conciliatory manner) : I am not going to say very much. I only with to enter my pro- test against the views which Mr. Whitley has been expressing at Dutton. When Mr. Whitley goes to Dutton he is supposed to represent the ratepayers of Stockton Heath and to express their views. (Mr. Whit- ley : That is what I do.) That is he is supposed to represent the views of the majority. You cannot get a community to take exactly the same view, and to be absolutely unanimous on anything. I am one of the Tree Planting Committee, and I happen to know that the tree planting meets with the approval of 90 out of every 100 people resident in Stockton Heath—(bear, hear)—and I think it is the duty of our District Coun- cillors to represent the views of the 90 in preference to the 10. I arms sorry Mr. Whitley has taken this line when he gets to Dutton. We should have appreciated his action better if he had commenced his opposition at this Committee, when we cotild have used argurnants and put our case before him and I have some confidence in thinking he would have been induced to take a I different view from that which he has expressed. But he did not do that. He went over our heads, pushed us 1 on one side and ignored us. He has not taken the views I of the Committee and has gone and made certain state- ments at Dutton which, put in recent language, are terminological inexactitude. Mr. Whitley, when he goes I to Dutton, meets another class of gentlemen who are pleased to believe,and ought to believe what he says, as they ought to take it that he is there expressing the; views of the majority of the ratepayers of Stockton' Heath. I hope and suggest that the Chairman and the Clerk will convey to the District Council the feelings of this committee that Mr. Whitley does not represent the views of this committee and of the parishioners of Stockton Heath. (Hear, hear.) I don't Want those gentle- men to be misled. If we know,and we do know they are being misled it is our duty to acquaint them with the real feelings of the people of Stockton Heath." (ilelr, hear.) Mr. Clarke concluding by moving a resolution in aecordance with his suggestion._ . .

Mr. J. W. Bouchier seconded. He thought that when Mr. Whitley, at the last Council meeting, go.t the ques- tion referred to the Parochial Committee, it would have been an act of grace upon his part to have seen how the Committee proposed to deal with it before he again brought the matter before the District Council, pre- pared a long speech, and had the insult put upon the village of the Highways Committee having immediately appointed to pay a visit of inspection to the village. (Hear, hear.) Mr. EL J. Westbrook associated himself with all that had been said. He would like a point cleared up upon which he had some don ,t, as to whether a Mr. Whitley who appeared at Dutton was their Mr. Whitley, because the Mr. Whitley who appeared at Dutton, judged from the newspaper reports of which he said, was quite a different person from the Mr. Whitley who appeared at the Parochial Committee. "At our last meeting" continued Mr. Westbrook, " Mr. Whitley was quite agreeablelto what was being done,subject to some small matters being settled. Then a Mr. Whitley appears at Dutton with law and no logic, reads a learned dis- quisition upon various matters and, as 'Mr. Clarke says, misrepresents us." Mr. Frank kVarburton expressed himself quite in accordance with everything which had been said. Mr. Ashton suggested that the proposition should be il to the effect that the District Council be informed that the statements made by Mr. \Vhitley did not represent the opinions of the ratepayers of Stockton Heath, Mr. Whitley: I would like to know who is responsible for the highway? Mr. Pilling: The District Council. Mr. Whitley: Not the Parochial Committee? Mr. H. J. Westbrook: They never claimel that. Ur. Whitley: Nor the Tree Planting Committee? Mr. Pilling: They don't assume that. It is no use asking the question because the Highways Committee gave permission for the trees to be planted. Mr. Whitley: My reply will be short because I conscientiously believe that I have done my duty to a great number of the ratepayers who have come and com- plained to me about the trees being planted on very narrow footpaths. People who have been in favour of them have not come to me about it, and therefore I laaveibeeu doing my duty to those ratepayers and they are a great number who come daily.sometimes three or four at one time and complain about the trees. Iqa a tell Mr. Westbrook I have not appeared in two chatacters, one here and another at Dutton. Mr. IVestbrook : I simply state my impression. I certainly believe it. Mr. Whitley : I simply moved that no trees be planted—although I ass in favour of trees being planted , in proper situations—on footpaths not less than eight I feet in width. I simply objected to the guards and the objectionable spikes on the top of the guards. We know very well, and no one can contradict it, that there has been damage done by these spikes. I can bring people who will say so. Both garments Land umbrellas have been torn. Mr. Clarke : They are' chaffing" you. I know it. 1 Mr. Whitley ; It is a fact. Mr. Clarke : It is a fact that they are " cha'llng " you. Mr. Whitley : I can bring them. Mr. Clarke : Oh, it is perfectly true that a man tore his umbrella, but the man blames himself, not the tree. He is only making a" mug" of you. Mr. Pilling: If your motion had been carried it I would have meant that we would have had no trees. Mr. Whitley : There is more than one footpath eight feet wide. I have been convinced that lam acting on behalf of a large number of ratepayers and in doing that Ilhave been doing what 'think is my duty to them. T have told you repeatedly I am not against the beauti- fying of the village and the planting of trees. I was the first to bring forwatd a resolution that trees should be planted, and also planted a tree opposite my house. , That shows Tam in favour of beautifying the village, I but no sensible man will allow trees to be planted upon I footpaths two or three test wide. Mr. Bouchier : What footp iths are two or three I feet wide. I Mr. Whitley would not answer the question when I appealed to do and for a time could not proceed. Mr. H. J. Westbrook : It is his usual misrepresenta- tion. A Voice : He is not at Dutton now. Mr. Whitley : I ask the surveyor what is the width of the footpaths where the kerb-stone is being moved at the present time? It makes no difference to me whether lam at Dutton or not. When I brought the matter up on one occasion I was insulted and told I did not know what I was talking about. (Mr. H. J. West- brook : Probably you deserved it.) What is the use of bringing things here when I am insulted and told I do not know what I am talking about. T take them to sensible men, not to the Parochial Committee. (Several members : " Nonsense.") 1 Mr. Whitley: The chairman here will bear me out. Good-night gentlemen. As he left the room Mr. Whitley said : I have not told any untruths at Dutton. I have been candid and straightforward. I hope you will come to my house and have a cup of tea or coffee. Mr. T. R. Westbrook: Go and play marbles. You are worse than two "kids. Mr. Whitley then left the roolia, and with the approval of the resolution suggested by the Clerk the meeting closed.

div.head: LIBERALISM IN THE KNUTSFORD
div.p: LIBERALISM IN THE KNUTSFORD
DIVISION.
Mr. A. J. King's Victory Celebrated.

The victory achieved by Mr. A. J. King, M.P., in the recent eleotion in the Enutsford Division was fittingly celebrated on Saturday when a meeting of Liberals in the Division was held at the Royal Botanical Gardens, Manchester. Almost a thousand of Mr. King's sup- porters assembled to welcome him, the number includ- ing a representative attendance from Stockton Heath. In his annual report, which he presented at the annual meeting of the General Council held in the afternoon, i Mr. J. B. Thistlethwaite said "The preliminary educa- tional work done by the association at very great sacrifice and expense has contributed in no small measure to the success, and the enthusiastic work of the members in the various localities has aided to bring about a victory which must rank as one of the finest in the country. Having won the seat every nerve must be strained to keep it ; there must be no over-confidence and no slackness of organization allowed to rob us of the fruits of the glorious victory. It was evident during the recent contest that general conditions were favourable, and assistance was rendered by some whose • support on other occasions might not be so active ; therefore, whilst for the moment there is no battle in prospect, it is more important than ever to keep this associatiou strong and efficient. The various district branches are earnestly exhorted to keep on foot their organization and to work even now at the Improvement thereof.

The report was adopted on the motion of -Mr. Thistle- thwaite. seconded by Nlr. Lloyd Jones. On the motion of Mr. King, seconded by Mr. H. P. Cr rag, Lord Stanley, of Alderley, was unanimously re-elected president of the Association. The vice-presidents were re-elected, and Colonel Brocklehurst, M.P.•for the 'Macclesfield Division, and Mr. W. C. Dunkerley, of Mere, were added to the list. - Mr. Longland moved the appointment of the follow- ing :—Mr. A. P. Greg, chairman of the Executive Com- mittee; Mr. H. L. Goodson, vice-chairman, in the place of Mr. R. Winfield, who retired ; Mr. Lonsdale Broderick, hon. treasurer; Mr. J. B. Thistlethwaite and Mr. R. H. Owen, hon. secretaries; Mr. J. Arnold Thompson, hon. auditor.

Mr. Hibbert seconded, and the appointments were ratified. After tea in the exhibition room, a meeting was held at which Lord Stanley again presided, and amid cheer- ing presented Mrs. King with a silver tea caddy, in commemoration of Mr. King's success. Mrs. King briefly replied. Their gift would certainly be long treasured and would remind them of the happy days spent in touring around seeing their friends, as she hoped they would often do in the future. I Ma. KING •M.P., AND CURRENT poLines. Mr. King, M.P., who was received with the singing of" He's a jolly good fellow" expressed his pleasure at meeting so many of his constituents. Speaking of the work of the Government he said a private members's IBill dealing with the reform of the system of land tenure passed its second reading on Friday night, and was accepted in principle by the Government. That was only a small instalment, but they looked for a much larger and more comprehensive measure to be brought in by the Government next year. So far the principal Government business had been to present to the House of Commons two enormous Budgets for naval and miltary expenditure. There was a strong feeling of regret in the House that those estimates had not been much more greatly reduced. Members, how- ever, quite appreciated the difficulties of the new Ministers. They had to accept practically the esti- mates as framed for them by their predecessors,and had not had time to consider carefully any scheme by which they could be greatly rerluced. There were many hundreds of members in the House who would not be content to see these Budgets so Large next year. An end must be put to the senseless competition between the Great Powers of the world in the building of ilnavies. They must get some definite pledge from the ;Government that they would approach those Powers, land he believed they had every intention of doing so. IHe should like to have a definite statement from them, I either at the Hague Conference or in some other way, that they would put before the great Powers some definite proposals for the cessation of the spend- ing of money for those enormous armaments. 'Last week a resolution was introduced by Mr. W. H. ILever in favour of the payment of members of Parlia- ment. (Hear, bear.) He (Hr. King) did not vote for the resolution ; he had no clear feeling on the matter. Throughout the campaign he had never a single ques- Ition on the point, and therefore he felt it was not a pressing question with the electors, although he remembered a great deat deal was said about economy and the reduction of expenditure, and in the face of that be did not think he could go and vote for the very first Act of Parliament to put £200,00 in the pockets of themselves. In principle it was no doubt a right thing to do. Whether it was the right moment and whether it would work out in practice as well as it did in theo,T, he was not prepared to say. The Prime Minister said he had neither the time nor the money to carry it out just yet, therefore he thought he might refrain from voting. Before the Bill came before the House he thought he might get his constituents' views ' and make up his own mind as well. (Hear, hear.) If they had patience for only six months he was sure the Government would by than justify the confidence which the country had passed in them. (Applause.) A vote of confidence in Mr. King was carried.

div.head: Ragged School.,
div.p: Ragged School.,

On Monday evening some 350 children were enter- tained to a substantial tea through the kindness of Mr. and Mrs. J. Charlton Parr. The arrangements were carried out in connegtion with the Ragged School, and the workers were well repaid for their trouble by the evident enjoyment of the children. The tea was followed by a short entertainment, and as the children left for home, an orange was given to each one. The treat is one that Mr. and Mrs. Parr have for some time made an annual event, and if some other of the local sympathisers with the poor could see for themselves the very real appreciation of the good things provided, they w mid probably feel impelled to imitate so excellent an example.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

THEFT FROM THE MARKET. At Warrington on Nfonday Fanny Floyd. Stephen-st., was charged with stealing from the stall of Joseph Frisby, in the market. on Saturday night, a pair of girl's boots, of the value of Ss. 6d.—The Chief Con- ' stable said a friend of the prisoner's went to the stall and bought a pair of boots. She was accompanied by the prisoner and while the purchase was being made, prisoner was seen by another stallholder to pick up a pair of boots and cover them with her cape. and walk away. The assistant was informed and he followed the woman who denied having any boots. They were found in her possossion and she thea wanted to pay for them. She had no need to steal haing a marrie i woman with a good hushand.—Prisoner. who asked the Bench to "have mercy on her," was fined 104. and costs. WANTON MISCHIEF. George Hewson, of no settled ahole, was charged at the Warrington Police Court on :Monday, with breaking a plate-glass window at the Crown and Sceptre, Butter- market-street, on Saturday night, doing damage to the amount of Rt.—The Chief Constable said that Mr. Walsh was in the house when he heard a crash of glass • and found that a plate—glass window had been broken. The prisoner went straight towards P.C. Hewitt and said he had broken a windoW. He picked up a brick and deliberately shied it through the window. The man had ahsolntolv no reason for doing it. and it WRS a piece of wanton mischief.—P.C. Hewitt said the prisoner had no money and wanted to be locked up.—He was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour.

div.head: C. J. STRAW'S SUCCESS. International Triumph.
div.p: C. J. STRAW'S SUCCESS. International Triumph.

It is only a few weeks since C. J. Straw, the wonder- ful Winwick runner, came out of his shell, so to speak but few cross-country men have achieved a record equal to the one he has established. A comparatively un- known man at the commencement of the season he, a few weeks ago, carried off the Northern Counties championship with ease, a fortnight later secured the first place in the National cross-country race, and on Saturday crowned the record by arriving home two hundred yards in advance of Parce in the International contest at Newport. Saturday's race was the hardest of the three. Not only was the class improved but the nine miles of the course was wet and heavy, rain falling throughout the progrecs of the event. Butter- field, England'e mile champion, took the lead, but at the end of two miles he had fallen behind, and Straw took up the running. As n the National event the race resolved itself into a struggle between the Winwick man and Pearce, and for a time the Southerner took the lead, butlivhen Straw again came to the fore the race was over. The gap between the two gradually increased and in the end Straw woo handsomely in 57mins. 32secs. Straw is not content to rest upon his laurels and this Saturday intends to place the Senior Liverpool Cross- country Association Championship to his credit. That he will succeed is open to little, if any, doubt.

div.head: TWO MONTHS FOR DESERTION.
div.p: TWO MONTHS FOR DESERTION.

Joseph Tickle, a St. Helens collier, who some time ago deserted his wife and four children when they lived in Gregson's-yard, was brought before the magistrates on Tuesday by Relieving-officer Cooper, who asked for the maximum punishment for desertion.—Tickle said he was in very poor health, and asked for the clemency of the magistrates.—He was sent to prison for two montbs, and the prison doctor would attend to him.

div.head: SALICYLIC ACID IN JAM.
div.p: SALICYLIC ACID IN JAM.
Important Case, at Warrington.

A case of considerable importance to grocers ems heard at the Warrington Police Court on Monday when William Henry Mayers, Powys-street, was summoned for selling jam which contained 2•1 grains of salicylic acid. The Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Hallawny) prosecuted, and Mr. McConkey, barrister, of Liverpool (instructed by Messrs. Masters and Venables) defended. The Depntv Towa Clerk said that on the 30th January the Sanitary inspector of the Corporation,Mr. Flood, purchased two pounds o! damson jam from Mr. Meyers. He divided the jam into three parts, and one was submitted to the Public Analyst, and it was found that the jam contained 2.1 grains nar pound of salicylic acid. The War Office in their contracts specially stipulated that no salicylic acids should be used in their jams ; and the Departmental Committc 3 on adulterated food, after hearing the evidence of the leading men throughout the country, recommended that the acid be not used to a greater strength then one grain per pound, and that its presence be stated. Mr. McConkey admitted the presence of the acid in the jam. Dr. Meredith Young, medical officer of health for Stockport, said, in answer to the Deputy Town Clerk, that when he purchased jam be expected it to be without salicylic acid. He contended that the quantity of that sample wonld not injure an ordinary human being, but it would hurt persons suffering from diseases of the liver, kidney, heart, or of the digestive system. A large number of people died from kidney and heart diseases every year. and it was obvious many people would be affected by drugs like these. It was not necessary to put salicylic acid in jam to preserve it. Dr.Gornall, medical officer of health for the borough, in enswer to Mr. Hallaway, said he entirely agreed vcith the evidence of the last witness. The present was only one instance from their experience of the presence of salicylic acid in jam within the last year or so. It was most desirable in the interests of the public health that some check should be put upon the continued growth of these preservatives in articles of food, because it was quite evident that if it went on there would be hardly anything in the nature of pre- served food which had not one of these chemicals added to it.

..„ Dr. Tnomas Roberts Bradshaw, physician to the Liverpool RAyal Infirmary, for the defence, said he had made a special study of the preservatives of food and of salicylic acid in particular. It was absolutely impos- sible for salicylic acid to haveany injurious effect what- ever in the quantity named in the summons. He thought it very desirable that jarns,which if not preserved would go had, should he placed on the marker in such a way that they were not likely to go had before the consumer got them, and that was especially important from the number of peor c3ople who used these goods. He had personally taken five grains of the acid per day for a month as an experiment, but they did not interfere with his digestion; in fact it was rather better. He explained an experiment which he had made by artificially digesting the white of an ego'. In one of the tubes by which the experiment was made, salicylic acid was placed but this did not interfere with the digestion. _ _ _ _
Mr. Hallaway: May I take it that the sum and substance of your evidence is that 2.1 grains of salicylic acid is not harmful? Witness: Yes.

Dr. John Lloyd Roberts, another eminent authority, also give evidence, and said he had made a special study of the action of drugs on the human body and of the use of preservatives in food. Adulteration with salicylic acid to the extent of 2.1 grains could not possibly be injurious to health. it was not cumulative. The Deputy Town Clerk: is the acid not prohibited in France?

_ . Witness: I think they allow it in articles that are exported. (Laughter.) The Deputy Town Clerk : They don't have it for their own use? Witness: I don't know. The Deputy Town Clerk : Do von know that it is prohibited in certain States of America? Witness: No: I don't. Mr. HArbert Davies. M.A., of Cambridg.e, a Pellow of the Institute of Chemists, and a consulting chemist in Liverpool, said he considered a preservative necessary in jam. He was being continually consulted by jam manufacturers who said they must use seine preserva- tive otherwise the iam went mouldy. They did not want a preservative. but they found they must have one. On the whole salicylic acid was the best preservative, and he advised its use.-13v Mr. Hallway : He*would not say that he considered the recomraenda%ion of the Departmental Committee were wrong, but ill-advised. They should have forbidden the use of salicylic acid altogether or allowed a reasonable amount. It was an unhappy compromise. Mr. ilallaway : Do you know that the War Office refuses to take any jam containing salicylic acid ? Witness: I did not take War Oflice jam asp, standard: Have you seen it? Mr. Hallaway: I have not, _ .

Witness : I have. (Lan ghter.l Mr. McConkey then addressed the Beneh for the defence, and quoted the case of Smith v. Wilsden, re- ported in the" Law Times," in which it was held that 13 per cent, of glucose in marmalade was not injurious to health. There was no evidence in the present case that the salicylie rvid was added to the prejudice of the purchaser. There was nothing in the jam more than was absolutely necessary to preserve it and the Preservative was not ininrions to health. He contended that the jam was of the " rltore, substance and quality demanded." There was not the slightest proof of any impropriety of any kind on the nart of the defendant. After a short absence from Court to enable them to drcide noon their verdict, the magistrates dismissed the case but declined to 3011 W the defendant's costs. The Deputy Town Clark : I must ask you to state a case for appeal.

div.head: HOW MR. JOHN BURNS WON HIS WIER.
div.p: HOW MR. JOHN BURNS WON HIS WIER.

Soon after his return from Africa Mr. John Bnrns (who is the celebrity in this week's " World ") was addressing a meeting on Clapham Common when the police dispersed the cro,vd and arrested the speaker. Among the onlookers was Miss Charlotte Gale, with whom Mr. Burns, as a boy of sixteen. had fallen in love before he went to Africa. Their marriage was out of the question at that time, but when the girl saw him marched off by the police her indignation fired her enthusiasm, and when the future Cabinet Minister was discharged by the magistrate next dsv he found that his one night In a police cell had won him a wife. Since then, throngh good and evil report, qrs. Burns has taken her place as the angel in the house, and it is she who has made his caresr achieve its utmost possibilities.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 17, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 17, 1906.

Was it any wonder that we had poverty, dirt, and disease in our great cities ? They might say that a great deal of this was due to the fact that people were herded together in bad houses more like cattle in pens than human beings, but he could testify after twenty-flve years' work in Liverpool that whenever a man had become sober and temperate and godly he had delivered himself from the slums, risen tci a higher plane of being, and found that the money he nsed to spend in drink enabled him to provide a happy home and respectable surround- ings. He thanked God for the wave of sobriety that was passing over the country as was shown by the fact Ithat in the last six years the drink bill had been reduced by 21 millions. That, however, was simply nothing, when they had present the enormous bill of over 160 millions. He was present at a great meeting when it was stated by one who had investigated the matter that of the 160 millions 100 were spent by the working classes. Then they talked about the unemployed and old age pensions. One half of the money that was spent on drink would enable them to pension off the aged workers, and to look after those who were poverty stricken through sickness and physical infirmities. Alcohol reigned supreme because the working classes had not faced the question. If they wanted a sober nation they must take their part in reducing the facilities for drinking. The Archdeacon concluded by appealing to his hearers. to realise their responsibilities as Chrisaans . . _ _

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Bible Class Opn Service.

An open service was held in St. Peter's Church on Sunday in connection with the Men's Bible Class, at which there was a fairly large 'congregation. Miss Plinston rendered" Lead, kindly light "and "Sun of my soul" in an effective manner, and Miss Violet Brown gave "Angels ever bright and fair" and "The volunteer organist." Mr. W. Booth ably sang "If with all your hearts." Hanley's Concertina Band was in attendance and gave two excellent selections. During an interval a short but interesting mldress was given by the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth. Special hymns were sung and at the close a collection was taken in aid of the Infirmary.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

The second meeting of the New Year of this prosper- ous society was held on Sunday last, when 21 new mem- bers joined making,/415 for the two Sundays. Mr. Councillor James Ball presided And spoke upon lessons from a picture he had recently seen in the Art Gallery Manchester: "The knight upon horseback and his two dogs." The animals were afraid of a danger before them, but the knight trusted in his God and com- mitted his keeping in God's hands. Mr. J. Harrison of Liverpool was the speaker, and spoke upon successes in the Christian life and the power of consecration to God and His service. The P.S.A. platform, he said, was for bringing men into close touch with God, leav- ing party politics and labour question, to those more directly concerned. Mr. Frank Brown sang " Calvary " and "The Radiant Mom". Mr. W. H.Payton,Mus.Bac., _
presided at the organ. Mr. J. Owen and the SecretAry took part in the meeting.

div.head: Legh-street Choir Sermons.
div.p: Legh-street Choir Sermons.

The annual choir sermons in connection with Legh- street Primitive Methodist Chapel were preached on Sunday by a student from Owens College, Manchester, whose morning text was " My times are in Thy hands " (Psalm xxxi. 15). Miss L. Snelling in the morning sweetly sang the solo" Queen of Angels." A musical service was held in the afternoon, and despite the inclement weather was well attended, Mr. E. Bridge presiding. The choir rendered a selection from Mendel- ssobn. The chorus" All men all things " was the open- ing item. Mr. J. FL Cerrin rendering the recit, and air, " Sing ye praise." The Misses A. Bridge and A. Wood- land (sopranos) effectively sang the duet" I waited for the Lord," the choir joining in the chorus. " The sorrows of death " WAS well treated by Mr. Corrin (tenor) while in the duet" My song shall be Matey Thy mercy," both he and Miss Bridge were heard to advantage. The choir rendered effectively the chorale " Let all men praise the Lord," while Miss L. Stronach,of Earlestown, sang the solo" A land of roses," and later also the solo " I will give you rest." Mr. E. EL Pearce delighimd the audience with his bass solos, " Arm, arm, ye brave " and "The light of the world." The chorale, "Thanks be to God," brought the programme to a conclusion. A large congrelation again assembled in Vie evening,when by special request the duet and chorus, " I waited for the Lord," was again contributed. Miss Stronach also sang," It is time for rest." Mr. Fred Podmore accom- panied all the selections.

div.head: Bawsey-road. Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bawsey-road. Wesleyan Church.

The prsscher a this church on Sunday morning was the Rev. Wm. gellor, wuo took for his text the words: " From henceforth let no man trouble me : for I bear in toy body the marks of the Lord Jesus." (Gel. vi., 17). In the evening the Rev. Sidney Pitt preached on "The LOV3 of Christ," his text being "Who loved me and gave himself for me." (Gal. 11., 20). He pointed out that the love of Christ_ dealt with mankind in an individual aspect, notes great-inasses or people, but one by one. in illustration of this he quoted passages from several poets embodying that view. He also showed by the example of the microscope and the details revealed thereby that the powers that were behind this Universe were certainly powers that went into detail. As instances he mentioned the veining of a leaf, the finish of the bee's sting, and tbe complex organism of the eye of a fly, as 'shown under the lens. Prom these he argued that it was not too much to expect arid believe that an intlividuil care and rive might be bestowed on human beings despite their countless numbers. At a meeting of the Wesley Guild on \fondly even- ing an interesting pacor was given by l'afr. W. Healey on The life of the late Thomas. Gnampness." :IWith the object of augmenting the fund for the decorating of the Lecture Hall a tea meeting organized by the Women's Bible class was held the other evening. The attendance numbered about 180 and the affair proved most successful and enjoyable. As a result about £6 has been handed over to the fund.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

Special services were held at this church on Sunday and were ltrgely attended. In the morning the Rev. A. C. Parker preached, his text being : When thou passest through the w 'tars I will be with thee ; and through the rivers they shall not overflow thee " (Isaiah xliii. 31. The Rev. .1. Manning preached in the evening on" The temptation of Christ ; its signi- ficance for to-day." The preacher took Christ's tempta- tion as illnstrating the inevita.bleness of the soul's struggle with evil that happened to the Bast of Men, the Perfect Man, and which was a necessary experience of life. It was a part of the preparatory process by which Christ was fitted for his mission ; without which even the Perfect Man would not have been fitted for the work he had to do. He bad to be hardened in the fires of temptation and went through the wilderness. He could therefose sympathise with the man who was tempted to-day. The same kind of experience was necessary to fit any man for useful work on behalf of his fellows. He must know by actual experience what the battle of life was before he could be of any real help to other people who were fighting it. Christ's temptation also illustrated the loneliness of the soul's struggle with evil. Christ fought the battle alone and every man to-day had to fight his own battle. In spite of all our friendships and relationships we were really isolated individuals and must pass through the deep experiences of life alone. The last point which the preacher urged was that Christ's temptation showed that we had an unseen Helper in the fight. St. Luke's account of the temptation showed that the Spirit was with Christ all through the Wilderness, and in the power of the Spirit he conquered. That unseen Helper was onrs.—The choir sang the anthem" Abide with me," solos being taken by Nti99 Taylor and Hr. Page. Mr. F. Hickman presided at the organ. At the meeting of the Wesley Guild on Monday even- ing a very able lecture was delivered by Mr. El. Stuart Page on a Mrs. Barbauld : the Warrington poetess." In a most interesting way be sketched the career of the poetess and presented a careful study of her works. Mr. Frank Harris presided over the meeting and at the close the lecturer was heartily thanked.

Archdeacon Madden on "Temperance and Manhood." "Temperance and Manhood " was the subject of an addren to men delivered in the Parish Church on Friday evening under the auspices of the Warrington Church Society by the Ven. Archdeacon Madden. There was a very large congregation,the body of the church being filled to its utmost capacity. Taking for his text the words " The fruit of the Spirit is temperance," the preacher, giving his reasons for taking an active part in temperance effort, said he had felt as most thinking and seriously-minded men had, that the national, sin of England was intemperance and that if he were a true ' patriot he should work to roll away the reproach from his nation. That intemperance was our national sin needed no proof. The 'nation which spent 160, 170 and 180 millions par annum in strong drink could not reasonably be called a sober nation. If the nation went on increasing in I intemperance, if the manhood of the nation grew less I sober what would be the outcome ?—national decayand degeneration. The only hope for the permanency of a ' nation or an empire was moral manhood and not material wealth or power. Great deers and mighty 'armies were powerless to hold a nation together if there was moral corruption in the very heart, in the manhood of the empire. Surely the fact presented to us by statesmen, judges and Labour candidates could not he ignored—that the whole strength of the nation, of its manhood and womanhood and family life, was being brought to ruin by habits of intemperance which w-re degrading in themselves and ruinous from a inational point of view. The Commission appointed to 11 deal with the question of physical degeneration stated with deliberation that one of the ,chief causes of the deterioration in the physique of the manhood of the country was intemperance. The pre:cher quoted the opinion of Sir Frederick Treves, the well-known surgeon to his Majesty, who stated that as a work pro- ducer alcohol was exceedingly ext-avagant ond, like other extravagant measures, was apt to lead to ILphysical bankruptcy. It was, said Sir Frederick, well own that troops could not march on alcohol. He was with the Ladysmith relief column and the first men to drop out were the drunkards. He also emphasised the folly of young men in the prime end vigour of their manhood taking alcohol. Continuing the Archdeacon pointed out how alcohol affected men intellectually and was largely responsible for the increase of lunacy in the country. To every man present that night who cared for the manhood of the country and the founda- tion of the e ripire which was in its manhood, his busi- ness was clear. He ought to banish alcohol from his table and make himself see that simply for his own sake ,he was better without that poison which was slow but deadly in its ultimate effects and would bring our manhood early to the grave as well as weakening it on its way to the grave. Alluding to the social side of the question, the preacher said that ao man who had any heart within him could consider the condition of things in the great cities of this country without feel- ing that he ought to do something if possible to bring about a reformation. He was prepared to say from figures supplied by Wm. Booth and the Right Hon. John Barns that from 60 to 70 per cent of the poverty of the country was due to intemperance. He believed that if they could solve the drink questionthey would solve some of the difficulties in connection with the unemployed. In Liverpool they were spending 3 millions a year in strong drink, whereas one million ought to satisfy the reasonable demands of reasonable people. The Liverpool magistrates had recently said that they wanted publicans not to serve women or chil-

div.head: Congregational Tea Meeting at Bold-street.—
div.p: Congregational Tea Meeting at Bold-street.—
The Needs of the Church of To-Day.

Success attended the annual congregational tea meeting in ,connection with Bold-street Wesleyan Church which was held in the schoolroo u on Tuesday evening. About 130 sat down to tea, the following ladies presiding at the tables :—Mesda nes alarming, Taylor, I. E. Barlow, Clegg, S. B. Stringer, Parkinson, Harris, Weaver, H. J. Dunn and Miss Benson. The following gave trays : nesdarne4 Toft, Stirling, J. Taylor, W. Cooper, Clegg, A. Silcock, S. Stringer, Barlow, G. Weaver, W. Silcock, I. Barlow, Stringer, T. Prince, Parkinson, Harris, R. EL Silcock, Bodle, Gregory, Halford, J. Fairhurst, Pattison, Nadin, Harris, Nelson, W. J. Dann, Daintith, H. C. Jones, Lingard, Miss Benson, the Rev. J. Manning, W.H.D., and Messrs. Arthur Isaac, R. Dale, PendleburY, J. F. Prince, W. Hickman, Brough, W. Isaac and F. Hickman. Afterwards a meeting was held, the Rev. J. manning , presiding. He was supported on the platfor n by the Revs. John Gunnell, F. Vaughan, and Walter Ainsworth of Liverpool. Several interesting sill-ems ware delivered. The Rev. F. Vaughr n. dealing with the religious outlook, said his reading of, general church life told him that one of the questions which thought- tntenen wereasking to-day was"Whea will the Christian Church again grip the masses as it did ia the days gone by?" History told them of the days when multitudes of people flecked together to listen to the old, old Gospel, and their hearts were stirred within them as the word of God brought conviction to their minds. Were they ever again to enter into the experiences of their revered forefathers? He thought they might hope ; he thought they might pray ; he thought they might have confidence that that would be the case. Individual effort, however, was necessary befare they could exp )ct an answer to their prayers and the fruition of their hopes. They must re-learn the old lesson that they were not so much the recipients of divine grace as the disooneers of divine blessings ; they must not be reservoirs so much as channels for the spreading of IGod's grace throughout the world. If they were to have I a real revival it would not come from either pulpit,pew or prayer meeting. It would come from an individual realization of the grace and goodness of God, and their object must be to live the life of God ; to live in daily and hourly touch with Him. they needed that self- emptyi ig experience so manifest in the lives of Christ and the Apostles—the pouring out of one's life for • Ow benefit of their fellownieu—and they must cultivate thlft frnitful, overflowing Christian life that had its overflow among the masses. (Applause). The Rev. JOHN Guesetr, in the course of an interest- ing address said the church which contented itself with defending its own was in a poor way, and it would not be long before it had nothing to defend. The surest way to defend the church was to enter upon the most vigorous aggressive work it was possible for Caristian ingenuity to devise. (Hear, hear.) It was by advanc- ing in the work of God that they could best defend what they now possessed—the whole life of the Chris- tian Church depended upon her aggressive action, and they must, as a church, kindle and maintain an enthusiasm for that work. (Applause.) The Rev. J. MANNING, in presenting the financial 'report for the year, said the income amounted to £359 14s. 3d. and the expenditure to £370 53. 33., leaving a deficit of £ll 2e. 53. Compared with former years he thought that they would notice that that was s atisfac- -1 tory, because it was not unusual for the deficit to amount to £3O or £4O. Bat that defloit of £ll. 9s. 3d. had to be added to past Micas, and altogether the total amount was £l2O 3s. 53. To wipe that off they pur- posed making a great effort in twelve months' time—an effart by which they hoped also to clear off the debt on the trustees' account, to renovate the chapel. and, he hoped—though this was their dream—to put in a new organ. (Applause.) Bold-etreet was a great centre—it was an ideal spot for the great central church. A church should not live for its own sake only, and so they had those central premises for the good of the town, and must see to it that they took full advantage of their opportunities. He was delighted with the stlecoSs of their Saturday night concerts, and was hopeful of I further aggressive work. He hoped they might be able to do something in the way of a Men's Institute. (Applause.) If they could get the young men on their side there was great hope, and he trusted they would go on with their work for the raising of the masses. The Rev. WALTER AINSWORTII Of Liverpool, said they were all there pledged to bring about what Christ died for, and every. church had its work to perform. Their supreme mission as the saving of souls, but they were also concerned in other things. They were con- cerned in everything that went to the forming of char- acter, and because their supreme work was thesalvati of the world it need not mean that they should neglect the mnsical side of life, or the intellectual or literary side. They must be an aggressive church. The moment they shut themselves from aggressive work, from that moment their decay would set in. Their churches above .all must be vigorous, earnest and enthusiastic, and they must remember that God expected the best services they were capable of rendering for the salvation of His people. The great inspiration of their work was the fact that there was nothini too sunken or down-trodden to be uplifted by Christianity. The great thing needed to-day was individual effort. The service di the Church's best and most napable and devoted men was needed for spiritual work. First and foremost they wanted the baptism of the Holy Ghost of all who were members of the Church and that would bring new life into the Church. All the rest would follow. (Applause). During the evening a song was contributed by Mr. Osborne and a violin solo by Sliss Taylor. At the! close a cordial vote of thanks was passed to ' all who had oontributed to the success of the gathering on the proposition of Mr. G. WEAVER, seconded by Mr. F. HARRIS.

div.head: TEACHING PROFESSION.
div.p: THE TEACHING PROFESSION.
Warrington as Compared with
Other Towns.

Interesting uomparisons of the conditions as affecting the teaching profession in Warrington and the other towns in the country are furnished by the handbook of the National Federation of Assistant Teachers which has just been issued. With regard to the salaries paid to male teachers by provincial authorities the Union scale is as follows :-Ist year of service+, £9O; 2nd, £95; 3rd, £100; 4th, £110; sth, £l2O ; 6th, £l3O ; 7th, £140: Bth, £l5O ; 9th, £160; 10th, £1.70 ; 11th, £lBO ; 35 years' total, £5.765. The authority which' comes nearest to this standard is Eastbourne, the teachers in the service Of that committee commencing at £95 and rising to a maximum of £165. The total for thirty-five years' service is £5,620. Warrington stands forty-eighth on the list of 275 authorities, the scale here being :-Ist year. £B5 (double !firsts begin £5 higher) ; 2nd, £9O ; 3rd, £95 ; 4th, £lOO ; sth, £lO5 ; 6th, £110; 7th, £115; Bth, £125; 9th, £135 (£lO extra for degree) ; 10th, £ll5 ; total for thirty-five years, £4,370. Me Union scale for female teachers is :-lst year, £BO ; 2nd, £B5 ; 3rd, £9O : 4th, £95 ; sth, £lOO ; 6th, £lO5 ; 7th, £llO ; Bth, £ll5 ; 9th, £125 : 10th, £135 ; 11th, £145 ;35 years total £4,665. Barry is first on the list with a total of £4,320. Warrington stands 25th, the scale being :-Ist year £7O (double firsts being £5 higher) ; 2nd year. £75; 3rd, £BO ; 4th. £B5 ; sth, £9O ; 6th, £95 ; 7th, £lOO ; Bth, £lO5 f£lo extra for degree) ; 9th, £110; 10th, £115; 35 years' total, £3.800. With regard to non-collegiate teachers, it is felt that so long as the college accomrnodation ic insufficient for the number of teachers required, and the abscence of a Con- science Clause for the Training Colleges debars some from receiving professional training in those institu- tions, these teachers should be remunerated at the same rate as collegiate teachers, and should not be pecuniarily penalised as many have been in the past. Moreover, the Board of Education has removed from the Code the distinction between college trained teachers and non- college trained teachers ; the vast majority of both classes have been apprenticed to the work of teachiug ; both have nassed the same examination, and both count on the staff for the same number of scholars. The atten- tion of members of Education authorities is, therefore, particularly called to the great monetary Ipss (as shown in accompanying tables), which is still sustainer] in many planes by non-collegiate teachers, in the hope that they will speedily take steps to minimise the great injustice under which these teachers still sniffer. It is shown that in Warrington the loss sustained by non-collegiate teachers in fifteen years was £2lO (men) and £125 (women), while the loss per year afterwards is estimated at £2O (men) and £5 women. From a table showing the rate at which increases of salary are granted it appears that in Warrington the commencing salary for men is £Bl rising by £5 incremets to £ll5 and then by £lO increments to £145. The Warrington 'YClass Teachers' Association is connected with the Federation sod has a membership of 138 as comcared with 54 in 1903 and 95 in 1901. The ISecretary is Mr. S. W. Jeffery.

div.head: Wigan Win at Warrington.
div.p: Wigan Win at Warrington.

Wigan who, like Warrington were knocked out of the Cup-ties in Yorkshire in the opening round, came to Wilderspool in tbe return Leigne match on Saturday. The matchalso counted in the South West Lancashire competition of which the Wigan men are the le ',dais. Warrington were handicapped as usual by the absence of injured players, Hockenhall being this time added to the list, Boardman, Sbugars, and Naylor were out of the forwards. Wigan brought a strong team and several hundred spectators. The gate was the best of the season, 7,000, notwithstanding a drizzling _rain. Teams and officials : Warrington.—Berry, hick ; Widdeson, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Taylor, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Lees, half backs ; Preston, Harmer, Heath, Thomas, Swift, Jolley, Morrison, and Belton, forwards. Wigan.—Nfason, back ; Leytharn, Jenkins, Price, and Lowe, three-quarter backs ; Thomas ald Anderson, half backs ; Hilton, Whittaker Brooks, Hootes, Barton, Watkins. AfcCaba, and Cohn, forwards: 1 . .

Referee, Mr. W. McCuicheon (Oldham) •, touch judges, Messrs. J. Gregory (St. Helens) end W. Jones (Runcorn). Preston started the game an 4 play was for some thee hotly contested in raidfield. Wigan displayed a great superiority forward and Anderson and Thomas were nearly always in possession. The spotting of the War- rington backs was, however, splendid and the Wiganers I were kept at bay. Eventually Thomas and Anderson I made a fine opening for Leytham, who we- held just inside. Lowe was next held up, whilst a fine break away by Price was well dealt with by Berry. Subse- ' quently the home backs combined and Dickenson effected a splendid run, and passing to Taylor, this player crossed to the open, and the ball baing quickly sent back, Taylor opened the sooting. Wigan rallied, and a cross-kick by Laytham ended in an equalising try to Lowe. At half-tlme the score was 3 points each. In the second half Wigan were early aggressive, and after Leytham had been checked he next at 2epted a pass from Jenkins, and punting over Berry's head scored a clean try. Warrington rallied in very plucky fashion, and the forwards heeling batter there was some effective combinations behind. A kick by Widdeson ended in a rush to the line where Mason saved grandly. Lees secured from the scrum and passed to Dickenson, the latter giving Taylor a nice chance which was not made use of. In the movement Dicken- son was injured and had to be assisted from the field. Thomas now went on the wing, and the forwards were still further weakened. ['he homestars were in a desperate mood end attacked so hotly that Wigan had to play an extra back on the defence. Isherwood had hard luck in passing widely to Widdeson after a good effort, while Harmer nearly scorci as the result of fine following up. Nothing but persistant touch-kick- ing saved Wigan, who finally ran out winners by 2 tries to one.

BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON.

div.head: How the Movement is Progressing.
div.p: How the Movement is Progressing.

The Beautiful Warrington Society is making encouraging progress and in order to interest the general body of townspeople in the work strong com- mittees areibeing formed in every ward. A meeting in connection with St. Au=tin's Ward was held in Cairo- street schools on Tuesday evening, Counoglor Dr. Josenh presiding.. There was a good attendance, includ- ing Canon Morley Stevenson, the Rev. C. Harvey Cook. 'Alderman Smethurst. Connellfors Fulton Smith and Wilson, Dr. Orniandy. Messrs. John Hesketh, F. J. Lord, John Fairiptrst, H. M. Ashton. J. Moore Murray, D . Hodge, J. Bayley, J. Lon gland, and Mr. Herbert I Gibson (hon. ward secretary pro tern.) Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from Mrs. Garnett of Penketh, the Rev. John Yonge. and Dr. Markel. Mrs. Garnett mentioned that she had put in a plea for Bank quay and Sankey Bridges where a few trees would help to beantify.

The CHAIRMAN observed that there was no doubt the ohjects!of the Society were very laudable, and they had his utmost sympathy and giipport. Next to their exist ence and the happiness of their home life was the pleasant appearance of the exterior of their dwellings streets, and surroundings. That was probably more important than anything else, and tended in the direc- tion of making their lives, their everyday lives, happy healthy and vigorous. (Anplsuse.) This wasa qnestions which concerned all equally, rich and poor, young and old, and he thought they could hearaly co-operate in the movement. He hoped that all present would do what they could to assist it and to make it a thorough success. If they expected erattd things all at once they would bel disappointed. Every little helped, and as long as they progressed in the right direction they should he satisfied. In a manufacturing town like Warrington they were apt to let things go by default and from bad to worse. Let them try to preserve the things that were beautifel. (Annlause.) Councillor Fuvroze SMITFI said the trae inwardness of the movement was not merely the planting of trees and window gardening, which to his mind were only the ontivard and visible signs. What they wanted to get at was the inner life of the families, so that what was seen outside would be a true representation lof the happiness and contentment within the dwelling \ (Applause.) There was a very wide score in the move • ment, more especially in connection with the interests of the children which were being brought into play. He thought there was nothina prettier than to see children taking a delight in making home not only pleasant and beautiful but happy andcontented. (Ap- plause.) The delight which it afforded people to watch the growth of 3 plant which they were carefully tend- ing helped to raise their thoughts from the ordinary routine of duty to something higher. By furthering the movement they would be helping in some measure to ameliorate the lot of the poor. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN FAIRHURST, hon. secretary of the Society, said they saw signs that the work of ' the society WP9 flourishing end although progress might be slow he felt certain that tbey would eventually sea some good arise from the undertaking. They would no donut be interested to know that the landlord of houses in Wake- field-street had offered prizes for the best kept gardens and several owners of property had offered to plant trees in streets. He was glad to find that the juvenile section of the society MI taking considerable interest in the movement, and if they could induce children to allow plants and flowers to grow they would have done a great deal. They had now,he was pleased to say, the co-opera- tion of the teachers of the day schools, and the total number of juvenile members was 2.110. (Applause). The other day he had an offer of all the surplus plants from a large garden distribution in the ward,principally in Parker-street. Arpley-street, and those streets where there was a. garden in front of the houses. He appealed to all present to join in the movement and thus help to briehten the lives of others. (Applause). Mr. J. MOORE MURRY said there could be no doubt whatever that if they could inculcate into the child's mind an admiration and care'for the beautiful it would be reflected in the home life.

• Alderman Sm ITURST said the depredations com- mitt3d hr some children in the Bewsey neighbourhood were really disgraceful and the Society would ba doing a good work if it could put a stop to them. The Rey. C. HARVEY COOK raid the Society were encouraging tree planting not simply as faddists but because they believed it to be an established scientific fact that the presence of trees in a town like War- rington acted as lungs to purify the noxious gases nod by absorbing them put forth sweeter air for us to breathe. Therefore they felt that in planting trees they were doing something to the enlarging and increasing of the public health. He did not see why the town should not be beautiful and the streets pleasing to the eye. They wanted to so improve the town that those who came after would say that their forefathers had a sense of beauty and perspective. They should pay special attention to streets which were sordid and mean, and help to brighten them by intro- ducing_flowers. .

Mr:H. M., ASHTON said he hoped the Society would do something for the abatement of the smoke nuisance. It was all very well to encourage the growing of flowers in the town, but he had personally found it very dis- couraging to try and caltivate flowers in the region of Sankey-street. The Rev. Caton STEVENSON said the question of smoke abstement was one with which the Society wr - very deoplv concerned and he thoroughly sympathised with Mr. Ashton's remarks. We own house Wit'S in close proximity to large chimneys which sent forth great quantities of smoke constantly and they could understand that he took an interest in the question. He could assure the meeting it was not being over- looked, and they would be interested to know that at the present moment they were engaged, chiefly through the instrumentality of Dr. Markel, in obtaining all the information they could upon the subject of smoke abatement and the different ways in which it might brought about. He urged the importance of the appoint- ment of a good strong branch in every ward which would send a hionthly statement to tbe general com- mittee of any improvements which they desirr 1. Before long they hoped to have an address from or of the principal authorities in the kingdom on the question of smoke abatement. (Applaufe.) THE COMMITTEE.

Mr. LotvoLAND moved that the following constitute the committee for the ward :—Councillors Dr. Joseph and Fulton Smith, and Messrs. John Hesketh, J. W. Hayward, Thomas Knowles, F. J. Lord, C. Madeley, R. Lee, J. Moore Murray. Thomas Webster, Edward Wallington, John Taylor, H. M. Ashton, John Walton, H. R. Horobin and Herbert Gibson. Mr. JOHN HESKETH seconded and the motion P7a4 carried.
A vote of thanks was accorded to Dr. Joseph for his services in the chair, on .the motion of Councillor FULTON SMITH, seconded by Mr. FeirhOrSt.

div.head: HORSE.TRANSACTION. Mrs. Crosfield Obtains £lOO Damages.
div.p: A HORSE.TRANSACTION. Mrs. Crosfield Obtains £lOO Damages.

At the Chester Assizes on Tuesday, Mrs. Gertrude Jane Crosfield, residing at Colwyn Bay, and formerly of Warrington, was the plaiutiff in an action for Ur: .ch of warranty in respect of a horse. The defendant was the Hon. Mrs. Ward. of Colwyn Bay, who is a well-known breeder and exhibitor of horses. Mr. S. Moss. M.P for the plaintiff, said that on May Ist, Mrs. Crosfl'ild called at the defendants stud at Old Colwyn and wt.% shown a pair of horses called Red Light and Chinaman. Mrs. Ward IVP9 away at the time, and the groom told her that the animals were quiet. Some correspondence passed between Mrs. Ward and Mrs. Crosfield. and the two horses were sent to Mrs. Cros- field on May 6tb. Plaintiff again asked Mrs. Ward's coaehman was he sure the horses were quiet in single and double harness, and that they would pass evelything, and received the teply "Yes." The horses were tried in single harness, and Mrs. Crosfield wrote accepting their. Mrs. Ward replied saying she was sure they woeld give satisfaction. iVf,rs. Crosfield sent, a cheque for £lB9 for' the horses. Subsequently both the animals were tried together. They went well for a short distance, 'out when a butcher's cart came up behind, the horse Chinaman began to plunge and kick. Plaintiff's groom jumped off the vehicle with a view to getting hold of the horse's head, but they were going at such a pace that le, was thrown down and badly hurt. Someone assisted in stopping the hoLie and then Chinaman began plunxing and kicking again, and behaving in such a way that his leg got over the poll. Ultimately the horse swerved and- the vehicle dashed into a cob. The horse received a gash in the chest, and after that Mrs. Crosfield considered it uncafe to drive it. It was subsequently found that the animal had been doing stud duty, and it Wl7, therefore, n^snited to drive in the public street: Mrs. Crosfield returned the horse, and claimed £ll4. Eventually she sent it to Crewe to be sold, and it only fetched 211 gs.—Mr. It. V. Bankes, for the defence, said that every word which Mrs. Wa-d used in describing the horse wrs absolutely true. The horse W 1,4 first put in barners in July, 1904, and it had, been driven repeatedly in and out of Colwyn Bay in single and double harness, and every conceivable fair trial that could be given it was given. The horse vv..a a handsome and powerful one, and won the third prize at the Dublin show, where it was driven by the defend- ant in the ling.—Counsel conterded that the sale of the horse at Crewe was an unfair one, and mentioned that the buyer had since refused £BO for the animal. In her evidence, defendant described the sale of the horse at Crewe as "ridiculous." The hearing was then rdjourned. The bearing of the action was resumed on Wednesday when a large number of witnesses were called for tb9 defence to show that the horse had been repeat lly driven about Colwyn Bayoncl was perfectly safe, having been converted into a gelding. Professor Willies Owen Williams, of Liverpool, ex- president of the Royal College el Veterinary Surgem7, said after a horse had left the stud six months there was no danger, and it was absolutely safe a onth after it had been converted into a gelding. The jut y found for the plaintiff, and awarded tb sum of £lOO.

Dear Children,— I am • very glad that so many of you have tried to solve the puzzles that appeared in this paper two weeks ago. Many ot you were quite right in your solutions, but I must award the prizes to the first two that I re- ceived. The names of the prize-winners are Miss Eva E. Foster and Miss Hannah Martin. Next week I hope to find space for more puzzles, as you all take such interest in them.

I am sure you will all be very interested andipleased to hear that we have now just 2,000 members for our League, and I hope that you will all take grt interest in "The Corner," and send me letters and contribu- tions. I have sent a prize to Fitzroy Lovell for his original story, and-also one to Gladys Kendall. Many of you seem to think, that unless your contributions are printed at once, that they are not accepted, but this is not the case. I receive so many that I must take them in rotation, and you must all wait your turn. I have received several con- tributions so badly written, and in pencil, that I could not possibly read them, and, of course, these I cannot consider at all. Next week I shall announce the prize-winners of the monthly competition for boys and girls, and I hope to give full details of our ElOwer Show Competition very soon. I shall award prizes next week for the two best short stories received; so you can all try for this. By "short stories," I mean about twenty lines. Remember lam no longer giving post Card . albums for lists of new members, although anyone wishing to join our. League is welcome. ‘,cith all good wishes from UNCLE NED.

-- Dear Vncle,—l amending you a con- tribution, and, as it is the first, I hope you will appreciate it. I am in Standard VII. at school, and I am pleased to say that I have several of your members as school- mates. I have been a member for a long time, although I should like my name pub- lished in the "Corner," as it has not been yet. I received a pretty blotting-pad from the Hovis Company, at Christmas, and I hope to secure one of your valuable prizes.— I am, dear uncle, yours sincerely, LESLIE MORGAN. •
PRIZE CONTRIBUTION FROM • FITZROY LOVELL.
THE THREE FISHES THAT HAD THREE WISHES.

- I A few years ago three fishes lived in a place called Seawater. These three were brothers, and their names were Jack • Mackerel, , John Mackerel, and William Mackerel. ' Jack, the eldest, was a large fish, and a great fighter, but he was a cowat..!ii Jchn s qualities were no better than his brother's, for he was not only a coward, but a bully also. He would swim away from a large fish, but would buily a small one. I.lTilliam, who was called Bill, was a quiet fish, and never got, into scrapes like his brothcrs, and, beca\use of this, they would torment and chaff him. One morning the brothers woke up, each with a dream to tell. Jack .said he dreamt that a fairy came and said: he could have three Wishes. John and Bill looked at him in surprlse for they had dreamt exactly the same thing. After a dis- cussion, they agreed to wish, and see if they really could have three wishes; so, with the same, Jack started wishing as follows: First, that he could have six fish to fight with; second: to see. an octopus; third, to have as much as he could eat a the things he liked best. Then John wished this: First, that twelve small fish would come for him to bully; second, to have a nice fresh worm to eat ; tliird, to see one of the great land monsters. Bill's turn had come now, and the brothers asked what his wishes were; but he said .he was quite happy, and did not want anything at present at which the two burst out laughing, and called him a duffer.

Nothing came of their, wishes that day, but, on the break of the next .day, Jac-k was roused by six mackerels, that said they had come to fight him, at which jack took to his heels—l mean his tail. Suddenly, as he was rushing round a corner, he banged into an octopus, which took hold of him and put him in a cage made of seaweed. There the octopus started poking him to see how fat he was, but in a .few minutes the octopus growled, "I must feed you up a bit, and you'll make a nice meal.' Jack, terri- fied by this, banged against the seaweed in vain attempts to get out, while the octopus made the water foam by his laughter. Then wL the terrible giant of the seas offered him a lot of nice tempting things, but Jack did not eat them. That is how Jack's wishes t were realised. (To be Continued.)
