CONTRIBUTION FROM GEORGE KIRK. 4 LESSON IN PATIENCE. Spot, you must be patient, sir; From your post you must- not stir. No, you need not Wag your tail, Wheedling arts will not avail. Till the proper time is come, Spot, you shall not have a crumb. Wait a bit. Patience is a virtue, Spot; From my copybook I got That wise thought, which pups like you Ought to pay attention to. I am nearly at the end Of the last new " Children's Corner." - Wait a bit. How the editor would stare, If he saw you on my chair, Reading his new Children's Corner " Galing at the cake, I mean! Can you catch? Now, let me see— I will just count one, two, three— Here's a bit.
PRIZE CONTRIBUTION FROM GLADYS M. KENDALL.
THE DOG AT HIS MASTER'S GRAVE "Faithful even unto death." .A TRUE STORY.

In the parish of St. Olave, Tooley Street, Southwark, the churchyard is detached from the church, and surrounded by high build- ings, so that no one can get in except by one large closed gate. A poor tailor of this parish, who died, left a small‘cur dog that would not be consoled for his loss.. The little animal would not leave his dead master, not even for food, and whatever he ate had to be placed in the same room with his master's body. When the body was removed for burial, this faithful attendant followed the coffin. After the fttneral, he was hunted out of the churchyard by the sexton, who, the next day, again found that the animal had made his way by some strange means into the enclosure, and had dug himself a bed on the Igrave of his master. Once more he was hunted out, 4nd again he was found in the same place on the following day. , The good clergyman of the parish, hearing of the circumstances, had him caught, taken home; and fed, and tried by every means to win the animal's affectibns ; but he was true to his late master, and took the first opportunity to escape and return to his grave. With true benevolence, the worthy clergyman. permitted him to follow the bent of his inclinations, and had built for him upon the grave a small kennel, which was supplied once a day with food and water. Two years this faithful dog lived in this manner, when death put ari end to his griefs.

THE WATER-CART. .` Oh, Charlie, brother, run at once And tell that man to stop; Why, look, the water from his cart— He's spilling every drop! "And yeti(oh, what a stupid man!) He does not seem to care; He never even looks behind, But drops it everywhere." . Said Charlie, "Now; Louisa dear, You are a little goose; The water from that funny pipe Is for no other use.. "Than just to keep rude boys and girls From riding on his cart; • Whenever they attempt to climb, He "turns it on right smart. "1 daresay, now, that cart contains Some valuable things; Perhaps • a golden watch, perhaps A• heap of jewelled rings: "And so-, of •course, he can't allow Rude boys to climb his van; . I think he must be very wise To think of such a plan. "But, sister, you are far too young To 'understand like me; But when you grow as big as I, Perhaps .as wise _you'll be." div.head: NOTES AND NE'
div.p: NOTES AND NE'
RAT FLEAS AS DISEASE CARRIERS.

Mr. C. F. Baker shows that the rat fleas of the warmer regions of .the earth are MOTO nearly related to human fleas than is the case further north. Human beings ar.f, thus more likely to be bitten by rat fleas in hotter climates. And if fleas act as carriers of disease from rats to humans the danger will be the greater in warmer regions.

div.head: CLOTHING FOR CONSUMPTIVES.
div.p: CLOTHING FOR CONSUMPTIVES.

The Practitioner states that as light has a fav- ourable effect upon sufferers from consumption, due to the bactericidal action of the rays, it has been inferred that the clothing of consumptives should be of such a nature as to allow the light to penetrate with the least amount of interfer- ence. For this purpose white stuffs are the best, and therefore it is contended that consumptives should wear clothing of white linen, velvet, coi- ton, or cloth.

div.head: AN ARTIFICIAL CELL
div.p: AN ARTIFICIAL CELL

An interesting example of an artificial cell is described by Stephan° Leduc in the " Comptes Rendus." It is formed by allowing a drop of sugar solution containing a trace of potassium ferrocyalkide to drop into a solution of sulphate of copper. As a result, the drop is covered, by a membrane of ferrocyanide of copper permeable* to water and impermeable to sugar. This mimic eell swells and grows, giving prolongations which look like radicles and plurnmules of grow- ing seeds. It is doubtless a series of chemical reactions which thus cause the drop to simulate the movements of a living cell.

div.head: SUN-SPOTS AND THE SUN'S SHAPE.
div.p: SUN-SPOTS AND THE SUN'S SHAPE.

From the —evidence of solar photographs it has been for some time apparent that the shape of the sun—as decided by its polar and equatorial diameters—does not remain constant, arra in the Astrophysical Jov,rnal Professor C. L. Poor gives the results of his examinations of helio- meter measurements 4:.%f the sun made at Gottin- gen Observatory during the period 1890-1902. From these visual observations (which, however, do not shew such large variations as the camera) it is clear that while at times the sun's polar diameter exceeds the equatorial, at other times the reverse is the case. 0 In addition the impor- .iant fact was ascertained (the Gottingen measurements were coincident with a complete " spot " cycte of eleven years) that a definite re- lationship exists between the sun-spot period and the period of the sun's variability in shape.

div.head: MIMICRY IN PLANTS.
div.p: MIMICRY IN PLANTS.

Dr. B. Marlot has described in the Trans- actions of the South African Philosophical So- ciety a remarkable case of what he considers to be true mimicry in plants. The famous travel- ler Burchell—after whom a well-known species of zebra is named—picked up on a bit of stony ground what he took for a pebble. On looking at it carefully, however, he found it was a plant belonging to the genus Mesernbrianthemum. Beth in colour and form it shewed a remarkable resemblance to the stones among which it grew. Another species has two leaves about the size of ducks' eggs, and which are of a brownish-grey colour, tinged with green like weathered stone. Another species has its leaves covered with white papery growths, which renders it like the quartz pebbles among which it grows. The ice-plant, which looks as if covered with bits of frozen water, is another species of mesembrianthemum. Plants like stones may also be seen in this country. On the South Downs, for example, curiously-shaped yellow and white fungi, looking exactly like the scattered pebbles of flint among which they occur, may often be seen.

div.head: MOLYBDENUM STEEL.
div.p: MOLYBDENUM STEEL.

Molybdenum steel, that is, steel to which a small quantity of the rare metal molybdenum has been added in the manufacture, is coming largely into use, says the Globe. The steel is found to be increased in hardness and toughness by the presence of a minute portion of this metal. MolFladenum steel is recommended for large forgings, marine engines, large guns, boiler plates, and high-speed tool steel. The ductile strength of the steel is also increased, which is important in wire-drawing. The bar to the increased use of niolybdenum steel is the rarity and high cost of molybdenum ores. The sulphide, known as molybdenite, is the chief of these, and although always met with in email quantities, is widely distributed. It is found in Cornwall, Cumberland,. and Leicestershire, in many European countries, in the United States, Brazil, &c. Though named from the Greek " molybdos," lead, molybdenum is a metal with very different properties. It is silver white, very infusible, and as hard .as topaz. The name, indeed, seems to have been given from the resemblance of its chief ore, molybde- nite, to plumbago, or\ " black lead."

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Edator as a guarantee of good ,faith.

Mr. W. Madden and Nonconformists. , Reply to Rev. eanon Stevenson. Sir,—l am indebted to you very much for the gener- ally excellent report which you gave of the speech delivered by me at the mass meeting of Catholics in the Parr liall on the 4th last. I wish, however, at once to say, that when referring to " Anglican clergymen standing on the brink" I have no recollection of having used the following words attributed to me by your reportet and wish to say that if I did, I had no intention of doing so : "If they once saw the way there would be such an Anglican movement as would show the Nonconformist body what was in store for them." I have spoken to the chairman of the meeting, Mr. Owen Toole, and to the Rev. Father Wilson as to their recollection of what I said, and find their recollection is the same as mine. Such words I admit are a veiled threat that if the Anglicans joined the Catholic Church the days of persecution and intoler- ance would be revived. They are quite foreign to my own views so frequently expressed during the late election. My view of the attitude of Catholics towards Nonconformists is that such attitude is generous and trustful. In marked contrast to the Anglican Church the Catholic Church believes that the Nonconformists are a body of good,Christian, religious men who are anxious equally with others, that their children should be religiously educated, and admits the magnificent fight that Nonconformists have made for civil and religious freedom all round. On this point, as indicative of the real opinion of Catholic laymen I quote from several addresses delivered during the present agitation, and within the last few weeks, by my friend Mr. Augustine Watts, M.A., once Catholic professor of Ushaw College,Durham, and at the present minute the intimate and confidential friend of the Catholic Bishop, Dr. Whiteside, and indeed of the whole of the Catholic hierarchy. At a meeting in St. Michael's Roman Catholic School, Liverpool, on the 18th of February last, referring to the Nonconformists Mr. Watts said "If I could reach the ears of the honest Nonconformists of this country, the millions of them who have religion at heart, and have done so much to uphold the improved conditions of our public morality, I would implore them to be no longer the dupes of those who pretend alone to know of what Christianity consists." And again at the great Catholic meeting at the Free Trade Hall on the sth March he said "I appeal to the Chris- tians of every denomination, to the Nonconformists whose religion is a sacred reality and not a mere cloak for political designs, to stand by us in this emergency, to pass a bucket everyone of them in the conviction that if our house burns their own will go to the fire." Men like Mr. Watts and myself, - even more than the ecclesiastical authorities have our hands upon the pulse of our Catholic people and know whither they are tending, and that they have the highest confidence and hope in the present Government. They are not likely to be led in the direction of the Anglican church or into any close alliance with them on this question by the angry utter- ances of a certain local Canon, who, being annoyed at the lead the Catholics are giving on this question, appears to have temporarily lost his head. To say that the Church of England is "the old Church of this country "and the Roman Church "an alien Church "is a piece of gratuitous effrontery and an ignorant mis- reading of history. But it was said in a temper.— Yours faithfully,
NVILLIA3/ MADDEN.

div.head: Mr. W. Furness Suggests Municipal
div.p: Mr. W. Furness Suggests Municipal
Reforms.

Sir,—While it is a laudable ambition to aspire to be a member of a Town Council, it may be that I shall hear the remark " That it is no credit or satisfaction to be a member of the local Town Council." It should be the ideal of all gentlemen who go to make up the governing Council of this ancient Borough to raise the tone of the Council to a more useful and a higher plane of thought and action than exists at the present time. A vast amount of useful time and opportunities are wasted in personalities of a character which reflect upon the dignity and personnel of the Council; which body should stand for all that is truthful and honourable in municipal life. There seems to exist an element of per- sonal animus between a certain section of Councillors which from a municipal standpoint is not in the best interests of the ratepayers they represent, and the sooner this is eliminated the better it will be for the town.

I am one who believes that municipal government should be conducted on broad socialistic lines—not the socialism that would equally divide the wealth of the world and give each individual their equal share. This principle is idiotic and impracticable, for any person who has through thrift and industry, acquired a stake in the country, will object to joining a body which would level down instead of building up. Socialism which raises a man to a higher plane is commendable, but the socialism which would reduce all to one social equality is pernicious and destructive of individualism and originality ; and not in the interest of the com- munity. The Council has lost one of the finest opportunities which would have made for this social millenium by the short-sighted business manner in which they bare carried out their street improvements. These have been carried out in a very piece-meal and extravagant way. Some 18 years hr.ve been occupied in improving Bridge-street, and as every little bit hasbeen done the property in close proximity has increased in value one hundred fold, and in some Cases more. The ratepayers' money has been spent in improving other people's property; for which the Corporation have had to pay an enormously increased value time after time—whereas if a comprehensive scheme had been formulated and powers acquired at first to purchase the whole as required for the improvement more than one half the cost would have been saved. In addition to this the land should have been retained by the Corpora- tion and let on say 60 years lease for building purposes. Had this been done the increase in the land value would have come into the coffers of the municipality and all grades of society therefore would have benefited. This would have been a first step to socialism of a sound and sensible character. I maintain that all land acquired by a Corporation should be retained by them so that its improved valuatien as time goes on may benefit the town and its people. As a Municipal Socialist I main- tain that the gas of the town should be the purest and best that science and skill could manufacture so that the atmosphere of the rooms where gas is consumed should noti be robbed of its oxygen. The gas should be supplied to the slot meters at no greater cost than is supplied to half yearly accounts. Every encourage- ment should be given to the poor to utilise the gas for light, warmth and cooking ; considering the profit that the Corporation is making out of its gas undertaking more, and cheaper facilities should be given to the consumer. The Building Committee should insist upon ,all houses that are to be erected having a bath fixed up; and if necessary an Act should be applied for compelling all builders to comply with this requirement. This convenience would have the effect of cultivating a taste for cleanliness and thereby generate more self respect in the lives of our citizens ; these are a few of the reforms which our Councillors should endeavour to consummate. I would also suggest that the Health Committee should insist upon the milk and food which we consume being pure and of an irreproachable character, and for this purpose they should insist upon frequent samples of the milk:and food stuffs being taken in the interest of the poor, who should have good pure and wholesome drink and food. They should go still a step further and insist that all milk sold in the months of June, July and August should be sterilized before retailed to the public. If this were done I ven- ture to predict that the infant mortality which is so prevalent in these months would, as a result of this regulation, be considerably decreased and many valuable lives would be preserved to the community—diarrhma and kindred diseases vailioh are so prevalent in these months would be considerably minimised. A great deal is talked about getting the people back to the land, but while this is a national difficulty and will require a national measure to remedy the On fortunate condition of things, still I think provision might be made in and around Warrington to cultivate a taste for horticulture and agriculture by providing allotments which should be situated so as to be easy of access. There should be no difficulty in this as whichever end of the town you look—North, East, South or West—land lies convenient to our hands. We have but to see the great and success- ful interest taken in the garden allotments in and about Leicester and also at Stafford to feel convinced that this is a step in the interest of the working man in our town. I have had the pleasure several times of walking through these gardens previous to and after the dis- tribution of prizes—which are given annually for the best cultivated allotments—and one cannot help being struck with the varied and useful character of the things under cultivation. It may be that from time to time after an experimental site has been taken that gifts of plots of land may be given and called after their donor. Our present Mayor, whose tastes are in this direction, could in no better way celebrate his Mayoralty than by conferring a gift of this character, to be called the Bolton allotment. In any case, the idea if carried out need not cost the town a single penny, but would be self-supporting and at the same time contribute a small moiety towards the rates as is done in other towns 'There are many end varied reforms which may be brought about in the present and future generation. I believe we have power as a Corporation to compel the landowners to lay out the streets before building operations commence; why,not go a step further—and this is astep which the Beautiful Warrington Society might very well press upon the :town—and insist upon all new streets being made of a not loss width than 50ft. and that the footpath be broad and spacious enough to admit of tree-planting of a sensible and use- ful character. Anyone who has travelled, as I have, through Germany and visited its numerous towns can- not help but be delighted with the beautiful way in which the towns are laid out and the trees planted, and also the great absence of smoke. A town before it

begins to plant trees must have wide and spacious streets and footpaths or else the trees, as in Stockton Heath,may be a common danger to pedestrians. Many re- forms of asocial and health-giving character might very well be advocated and brought to a successful issue with- outoas seems the tendency at the present day,to increase the rates, as it must be recognised that whatever goes to increase the rates, over and above a certain amount. must, of necessity raise rents, and lessen the purchasing power of the people, and therefore interfere with the prosperity and progress of the town.—Yours, etc., WILLIAM FURNESS. Sankey, March 15, 190 G. AP-

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

Warrington's inability to beat Wigan on Saturday was a great disappointment. The fixture is always a popular one, and as a rule the locals have no diffi- culty in taking two points out of the Wigan men at Wilderspool. But the team is not what it was. Illness and injury have decimated the ranks until the team which has to do duty is hardly recognisable as the one which won the Cup at Headingiey last April. To add to the misfortunes which time has somewhat inured us to, Hockenhall was absent on Saturday, and before the close of the match Dickenson received another injury which will prevent him playing again this season. ISfeanwhile our proud" A " team— the champions of last year and this—was getting a terrible gruelling at Wigan as the result of Jones sustaining a broken collar-bone. Troubles never come singly, and just now it is perhaps as well. Warrington have nothing to win and nothing to lose—except money— and if they can get all the catastrophes over with there may be better prospects and more good luck next season. Let us all hope so !

Though the result of the game on Saturday was a sore disappointment to Warrington people, they witnessed a rare good struggle in which the issue was doubtful right to the last moment. Good football,too, was not sacrificed to keenness, and there was plenty of fast, open play, which aroused the crowd to enthu- siasm. The hamesters were subjected to a severe attack right from the commencement of the game and nothing but the sterling character of the defence— which, at any rate maintains the traditions of the Club—kept Wigan from getting an early lead. Suddenly there was a remarkable .transformation. The home backs got possession promptly for almost the first time, and by beautiful combination in which Isherwood, Dickenson and Taylor shone, they pene- trated the visitors' defence with an excellent try. This success had hardly been applauded to the echo when there was another transformation. Wigan put ,on severe pressure, and a cross-kick by Latham gave Widdeson more than be could manage. Lowe beat 'him for possession though apparently off-side, and equalised. The interval brought about the next change, when the teams were on level terms.

It cannot be said that the home supporters viewed the opening of the second half with much cenfidence. Wigan were quite as smart behind as Warrington, and speedier on the wings,while the forwards simply dominated matters in a fashion totally new tu the Warrington pack. They quickly assumed the aggres- sive and took the game into the home quarter. Points were not cheap, however, and it is very unlike- ly that there would have been any more scoring but for the cleverness of Latham. He received a pass when by no means favourably placed. Speed carried him down touch to Berry, whom he defeated by a short punt and then secured cleverly over the line for a capital try. 'lt is to the home fall back's credit that he did not play the man. He could easily have upset Latham, and most custodians would have done so, but Berry played the game. Even now Warrington were not beaten. They made a better showing than at any previous part of the game and, by sheer grit forced Wigan to defend. They might have equalised through Taylor, but the latter ran the wrong way when given the ball and was tackled on the line. Several forward rushes quite broke up the Wigan ranks, but Mason or Dame Fortune saved them. When Dickinson had retired Warrington still attacked, but there was a want of finish noticeable, and Wigan retained their lead to the end.

The star artiste on the winners' side was Mason, the full back, who though kicking only half the length of Berry's ponderous punts, was never once at fault and saved the citadel repeatedly in the closing stages. Both halves wer3 very active and found the third line plenty of work, which was very dashingly accom- plished. Against such skilled defenders as the War- rington centres, the Wigan backs were frequently helpless, but they were always trying and always getting the ball. Their fore ards quite worsted the home eight in the packs, which is no credit to the latter even though Boardman and Shugars were still absent. It was not weight that did it,for I doubt whether Warrington were the lighter lot.. They were devoid of the Wiganers' "fire," and only wakened up when too late.

As I have already indicated, Isherwood sad Dickinson were in great form at centre, and it is a pity they Imd not speedier men than Taylor and Widdeson an the wings. The latter was the weaker of the two and seems to have fallen away from his Broughton form in remarkable fashion. He was not without opportunities on Saturday, and I was forced to the conclusion that " Widdy," though neat, was not effective. Brooks and Lees did not do so badly, while Berry played well in the rear, though not quite up to his Batley display, lie is improving in knowledge of the game each week and is rarely caught out of position by the ball.
Wigan's victory makes them practically secure of the West. Lancashire Cup, as will he seen from the position of the competing clubs in the appended table :
• Points. P. W. L. D. For Agst. Pts. Wigan Leigh Warrington 8 . 4 4 0 .45 29 ... 8 Runcorn Widnes 8 0 6 0 19 59 4 St. Helens

Wigan and Salford met at Weaste on Wednesday and the Wigan men gained a fortunate victory by 8 points to 6. Lomas played a great game for the losers but made a serious mistake on his own line which gave Wigan the match.

The second round for the N.C. Cup will be played to-day, the matches down for decision—on the ground of the first-named club—being as follow : Batley v. York. Brighouse Rangers v. Hull Kingston Rovers. Hull v. Keiahley. Oldham v. Halifax. Bradford v. Leigh. Salford v. Egerton. Leeds v. Broughton Rangers Featherstone Rovers v. Widnes.
Warrington's misfortune in losing at Batley is accentuated by the fact that they would have been

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 17, 1906
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 17, 1906

able to place a strong team in the field to-day. Fish and Harris are both pronounced "fit." How much the series of blunders at Mount Pleasant cost the club edit only be conjectured, but I think they would have made a bold challenge for the Cup again once the ranks were strengthened. Then too, the loss in hard cash must have been considerable, and receipts for the current season badly want a fillip. A share in the Leeds gate to-day should give a welcome lift to the exchequer.

Leeds and Warrington should have met in a league match at Leeds to-day, but the cup-ties have caused the match to be postponed till Monday. Meanwhile overtures have been made to Warrington and Runcorn to play a match to-day (Saturday) at Edge-lane, Liver- pool, in order to encourage the Liverpool Northern Unionists. Particulars are advertised on the wall

The Warrington team has been selected as follows : Berry, full back; Kenyon, Isherwood, Taylor and Widdeson, threequarters ; Brooks and Lses, half- backs; Preston, Thomas, Belton, Shugars, Heath, Harmer, Swift and Morrison, forwards. The list of the injured has been increased by the name of Jolley, who got hurt early in the Wigan match. This, no Idoubt, had something to do with the home forwards' poor show.

There should be a good" A " team match at War- rington to-day, when Radcliffe Rangers, the winners of the Manchester League, visit Warrington. They have an excellent reputation, but the side chosen to meet them should prove altogether too" hot." Fish and Harris are both included, and it is to be hoped that these two will enable the club t 3 finish the season in something like creditable form. The "A " team selection is : Knight, full back ; 'Fish, J. Davies, Cartwright, and Harris three quarters ; Lambert and Lloyd, half backs ; Ashton, Naylor, Forster, Bradshaw, and Lunt, forwards.

The heavy defeat by 22 points which the" A" team sustained at Wigan came as a shock to Warring- ton people, who have got so accustomed to the Champions' successful progress. Jones' injury early on, however, had much to do with the collapse, for the forwards were overweighted and Wigan had nearly all their own way. Luckily this, Warrington's first Combination defeat, does not endanger their position as Champions. They have only to get three points out of three remaining Combination games in order to secure the medals. Two of the matches are at War- rington, the one away being at Oldham.

The Works Competition opens on Monday, and particulars of the draw will be found in another column A valuable suggestion is made to obviate touch-play and scrummaging. Deliberate kicking into touch will result in no gain to the kicker.

I understand that my criticisms on the management of matters in connection with the Batley cup-tie caused considerable heartburning at headquarters, though it is not denied that a mistake was made in playing Lloyd. It seems to be the fact that when the team was first select6d, the contingency of Lees being unable to play was not properly'taken into account. Lloyd was selected as reserve half, and should have been played in that position or not at all. The primary error was in not picking a reserve three-quarter, and for this the full committee is to blame. The responsibility thrown on those members who ,accompanied the, team was a heavy one, and they were undoubtedly handicapped by the fact that there was no extra three-quarter chosen. I make this explanation to show that the three gentle- men most immediately concerned should not be debited with the full weight of responsibility for the fiasco. LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS.

J. F. Matthews, and Messrs. W. Bibby and William Roberts. The hon. secs. appointed were Messrs. J. Bibby, F. Atkinson, George E. Hayes and C. H. Cliff. BEWSEY WARD. FAIRFIELD wApD. • The annual meeting of the Fairfield Ward Liberal Committee was held in the Fairfield schools on Wed- nesday evening, Mr. George Walker presiding over a good attendance. Mr. Walker was re-elected chairman whilst the vice-chairmen appointed were Councillor Duncan, Messrs. W. Haigh, B. Farrar, J. T. Locker, J. Griffiths, and the Rev. H. Wall. Messrs. %V. fla.bberley and George Rushton were elected secretaries.

they became passive resisters and found they had got a conscience. They had paid for the same thing in taxes for thirty years but all the time they had not discovered it was against their conscienees to do so. There must,he thought,be something unreal in an agitation which based itself on a conscience which had been discovered only after thirty years. The proposal which was hinted at that Roman Catholics should receive 1 special treatment, and Nonconformists should have the 1 Undenominational teaching which satisfied them, while Churchpeople should not be allowed to have their faith taught, was abominably unfair. Continuing, the speaker said he was not prepared yet to become a passive resister, but he should be under certain circumstances. I Mr. Winston Churchill had distinctly said that passive 1 resisters deserved consideration, and that their acts in standing up for their consciences, even to the extent of allowing the spoiling of their goods and going to prison required to be recognized by an alteration of the Act. If that were so, passive resistance was no longer something which was opposed to the law and order of the country, but something which I was regarded by an English Government as an ordinary means of agitation against an Act which had given dissatisfaction to some people. If Parliament showed that they had regard to that movement he would feel justified in adopting the same tactics to secure an alteration of the law which should be just to him as well as to other people. Churchpeople eould make their voices heard and possibly adopt some action like passive resistance. They should be determined that whatever happened they would demand in future such 1 rights as would show the Government that they were I not going to sit down to injustice. The question would never be settled until they had the right to have their own children taught their own faith in every school in the land, both provided and non-provided. They asked for nothing for themselves that they would not give to others. (Applause.) The speaker concluded by moving the following resolution "That this meeting protests against any legislation (1) which would either establish, at the expense of the whole community, a form of nndenominational religion for all schools throughout the country, or would give to any denomination religious privileges not accorded to others ; (2) which would place the Bible in the hands of teachers whose belief in the Christian Faith and whose qualifications and ability to teach religion may not in any way be tested ; (3) which would alienate property held in trust for giving religious education ; (4) which would interfere with the power to give in school hours by the clergy and school staff (subject to a conscience clause) religious teaching in accordance with the Trust Deeds." Mr. W. P. JAMES seconded. Mr. C. TURNMR (headmasterlof the schools) and the Chairman supported the resolution which was un- animously carried.
Votes cif thanks to the Rev. G. R. Oakley and the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: EDUCATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE EDUCATION QUESTION.
Rev. F. E. Powell and " Undenominational " Religion.

In the course of a letter to the "Manchester Guardian " the Rev. F. E. Powell, Vicar of Sewerby, Bridlington and formerly vicar of S. James' Latchford says :—Dr. Clifford and his friends want the civil law to force" simple Bible instruction" upon all citizens. The conscience clause—which, I presume, they are will- ing shall continue—means this or nothing for our chil- dren. I sin one of the many who simply do not believe in this "simple Bible teaching." To me the term is speciously fraudulent to ensnare the unwary. What" Bible" is to be used—that of the Verbal In- spirationist or that of the Higher Critic; that of the Romanist or that of the Protestant ; that of the Unitarian or that of the Trinitarian. Some preconcep- tion of the Bible every teacher must have. Why there is no agreement as to the very version which shall be used, some preferring the Authorised, some the Revised and Roman Catholics the Douay. And the measure of the depth of the sincere conviction of a teacher—a Romanist or a Quaker, an Agnostic or a Churchman—is the measure of his disagreement in the" simple Bible instruction "of another. _

There are those, I know, who do not agree with me in this view. They think it possible to evolve "simple Bible instruction" where these differences do not appear. Let me grant it as possible. But, then, the very simplicity of this Bible instruction would be the measure of my disagreement with it. It is the teach- ing of a new sect—the sect of unsectarians. Let this section of our community, and those who are content that this "simple Bible instruction" shall be given, by all means have it for their children. Not for worlds would I deprive them of it so long as their consciences are willing to 'accept it. But let them ask us who do not believe in it to pay for it only as they, in their turn are willing to pay for that which our consciences are alone able to accept. This is "the alphabet of that long and hard lesson" undenominationalists seem unable to learn. . . . .

_ We denominationalists desire only to be treated like undenominationalists by the civil law of the land. Our demand is that the claim of both or of neither shall be impartially and fairly recognized. Is not this Liberal- ism ?—Yours, FRANCIS E. POWELL. Sewerby Vicarage, Bridlington, March 10.

div.head: Sermon by Canon Stevenson.
div.p: Sermon by Canon Stevenson.

Preaching at the Parish Church on Sunday morning, the Rev. Canon Nforley Stevenson, addressed a large congregation on the subject of religious education in the day schools. Basing his remarks upon Hark x., 16.. "And He took them up in His arms, and put His hands upon them and blessed them" he said there was no more touching passage in Gospel history than that in which Christ rebukedihis disciples for keeping children from Him. It was not only a touching picture but it con- tained a valuable lesson and from that time the Church of Christ had seen in that picture a duty .which had been placed upon Her to bring children to Christ and Christ to the children. He wished that in the season of Lent with all its solemn associations and serious teach- ing they could keep free from the noisy clamour of the controversial strife about religious teaching. He would he could have spoken to them that morning upon subjects which touched their spiritual life rather than upon that bitter controversy, but it was forced upon them not by their own action or wish but by others, and they dare not, for the sake of the children. refuse the conflict. Canon Stevenson proceeded to explain the growth of the present educational system— a system which, he said, was just and equitable, as it allowed religious education to be given in the day schools in accordance with the teaching of the body which built the schools. In Warrington, he ventured to say, there was not a child whose parents could not send it to a school where it could secure religious educa- tion in accordance with the wishes of its parents. He would like to call their attention to some of the dliii- culties and dangers which seemed to be ahead of them. While they did not know what the Govern- ment proposed there would be a strong move 'to have a Bill passed in the House of 'Commons which would make it impossible for religious I education to be given in the schools, whilst probably a form of simple Bible teaching would be insisted upon instead. Upon that he would ask them: did they think it just that the religious bodies who had been encour- aged to build the schools upon the distinct understand- ing that they should be at liberty to give distinct religious teaching, should never again teach their own religion? He thought that English people, in their Sense of right and justice, would feel at once that that was not just. He thought that one of the most clever devices put before the country was the expression simple Bible teaching." It did not mean that they would be entitled to teach the whole of the Bible, but that they would take the Bible as a reading book from which they would draw certain moral lessens such as truthfulueis and honesty, but they were not to teach a single doctrine in the Bible for fear that the teaching might give offence to someone. He said in all seriousness and , earnestness he could not conceive how they could do a greater insult to the Bible than to treat it in that way. To take the Bible in that expurgated manner and to give only moral lessons from it upon which they all agreed was to treat it as it ought not to be treated. They wanted their children to learn something moo than moral lessons. They wanted to teach them the truths of the Ci,ristian faith which they held to ba dear and sacred. He appealed to them earnestly not to be weary in the fight but by their induence and words to leave nothing undone which could be done for the cause of religious education.
At the request of the Rector a number of members of the congregation signed the National Society's petition.

div.head: MEETING IN ST. EARNABAS' SCHOOLS Passive Resisters Criticised.
div.p: MEETING IN ST. EARNABAS' SCHOOLS Passive Resisters Criticised.

A meeting of Church of England parents and others I was held in St. Birnabas, schools on Nlonday evening, the Vicar (Rev. .1. H. G. Hollingworth) presiding over a good attendance. Amongst those present were the Revs. L. N. S. Blakelock, Dr. Salts, and W. J. Gardner, The principal speaker was the Rev. G. R. Oakley, Vicar of Dearnley, RoFhdalo. After reviewing the Church's work for education, he contended that educa- tion embraced the whole being of a child—body,soul and spirit—and that Churchpeople had a claim as ratepayers and taxpayers to have their children taught the Chris- tian faith as they believed it. They were told that the Nonconformists were labouring under a great grievance. There was, he always admitted, one grievanee, and that was in the case of districts where there was only one school—and that a Church school—which the children were compelled to attend and receive Church teaching or no teaching at allots religious matters. But it must also be remembered that there ware other places whore there was only a Board school and where Church children who had to attend must receive either undenominational teach- ing or no religions instruction at allAVith regard to religi- ous " tests " it must be plain that teachers who taught religion must believe what they taught. Nonconform- ists said the Church schools were supported by the rates ! and no Dissenter could be headmaster in them. Church people said they paid far and above what they needed to pay for that choice of headmaster by having given their buildings in order to have that choice. If they gave their school buildings it was a very small matter that they should have taught half an hour daily the faith of the Church which built the schools by a person who believed what he taught.VVhose fault was it that theai was this Nonconformist grievance? They at St. LI trnabiLs' Church had built that school for the children of the neighbourhood and no doubt many Nonconformists attended it. There was a Church headmaster and the Churchpeople valued his teaching. Whose fault was it i that there was no opportunity for a Dissenter to become headmaster in a school in that neighbourhood? It was simply the fault of the Nonconfor nists who had not • built a school for their own children. Under the pre- sent Act they could build a school and throw it on the rates immediately. The injustice lay in the fact that Nonconformists sent their children to a Church school to save their own pockets and having sent their children there to be taught on the cheap—as far as they were concerned—for many years,they claimed as theirs the school for which they had not paid a penny. They were told very frequently that the Church schools were ruled by the parson or the priest. If that were true five years ago it was certainly not true now, as by the Kenyon-Stanley clause the religions instruction was placed under the control of six managers. The parson had therefore only a sixth of the power that he possessed prior to 1902, but he still had the same trouble in raising money, attending to the correspond- ence Sitc. One thing was certain and that was that, as Mr. Balfour had said, the day would come when the Act of 1902 would be considered one of the greatest Nonoonformists Acts that was evp r passed in the sense of removing Nonconformist grievances. It certainly reduced the power of the parson ; it brought in outside managers,and threw open many positions in schools which Nonconformists could not previously enter. Noncon- formists complained of the injustice of having to pay rates part of which went to the support of teaching of which they did not approve.Churchpeople said they paid in return far too large a suns by giving their buildings. There was, however, one way of avoiding that grievance which Nonconformists would not adopt. That was to let all the persons who paid ' the rates say what school their rates should go to. Churchmen could pay for Church schools and Non- conformists for schools of their own complexion. That course was suggested in Parliament three years ago,hrit 1 Nonconformists would not hear of it.lf it was true that Nonconformists paid for teaching of which they did not approve, the same was true of Chnrchpeople in regard to the Board schools. He objected most strongly to a jelly-fish religion with nothing definite about it.Church- people had contributed towards the Board schools with- out complaint for many years past. Yet the moment these people found they had to pay a very small pro- portion of money which went towards Church schools

div.head: MEETING IN ST. PAUL'S SCHOOL.
div.p: MEETING IN ST. PAUL'S SCHOOL.
Mr. A. J. Jolley and the Extremists.

A well-attended meeting of parents and others was held in St. Paul's school, Kendrick-street,on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. H. Smethurst 'presided and amongst those present were the Rev. W. Braoecamp, Canon Morley Stevenson, Alderman Smethurst, Messrs. John Rigby, A. J. Jolley, H. F. Greenough, H. Houghton, H. Collin, T. Armstrong, Critchley and Hayes. Letters of apology for non-attendance were received from Mr. L. W. Reynolds (treasurer of the school), Mr. C. S. Burgess, and Mr. H. J. Westbrook. The CHAIRMAN reviewed the history of the educa- tional question. So far as could be gathered from the utterances of men like Mr. Lloyd George it was the intention of the present Government to do away with denominational teaching, and as Churchpeople they must resist it. They must contend very strongly for the old system of denominational teaching brought up to date. It had proved its value in the past and he had no doubt that Churchmen would be willing to make sacrifices for the good of their chil- dren in the future. If they did not get their own way he hoped they would not adopt the line of the passive resisters. That seemed to him to be very like a dog- in-the-manger" policy, by which people gained what was nothing more or less than very cheap notoriety. I There would not have been any passive resistance if those people had in the past done their duty to the children of their own denominations. (Applause). • aft. Joux RIGBY" moved That this meeting approves of the principle that children should be brought up in the faith of their parents, and that the religious teaching should be given in school hours by teachers who believe what they teach and are qualified to teach it." Mr. A. J. JOLLEY seconded. He ventured to think that the great mass of the people of England, whatever their religious opinions might be, were sensible, moderate people, and the trouble that faced them was largely due to a few extremists. They had had a great deal of friction and he was afraid they would .have more, but if the usually silent mass of the people let it be known what it was that they wanted,then he hoped and believed that what they regarded an the absurd ideas of the extreme faddist men on either side—the narrow, intolerant people—would be set aside and that the wish of the sensible, moderate majority would prevail. He had worked in a friendly way with many Nonconformists. He might mention that on the War- rington Education Committee the religious difficulty had not arisen at all. They had got along extremely well because he thought the representatives of the Church of England, of the Nonconformists, and of the Church of Rome had been, as the majority of their fellow countrymen were,sensible and moderate and had worked together in a spirit of give and take. There was, he was afraid,a real danger that amidst the clamour of extreme people and the bitterness which too often arose out of it, many people would say " What is the use of bother- ing ? Let us clear religion out of the schools alto- gether "and the country would drift into a system of purely secular education. He thought that anyone who would try and esalize what secular :ducation pure and simple would mean in this country would shrink with horror almost from the thought. He contended there was nothing in the resolu- tion which any sensible man could take exception to. They did not want to ram their own opinions down other people's throats. They did not want to compel Nonconformists to receive instruction in the principles of the Church of England—they. were quite content that they should receive their own particular form of religious instruction—but Church people did demand that their children should not be deprived of the tights and privileges they had hitherto enjoyed, simply to gratify the whims of a few extreme people. They were not met there in any sense whatever as a political gathering. Education was of far too vital national interest to be made the sport of ,mere party politics. It ought to be above party, and in a move- ment like that Liberals and Conservatives ought to join loyally to defend what they regard as vital national interests. (Applause.) Alderman SMETHTRST supported and said that scarcely one of the passive resisters in Warrington had a school that he could use for purposeslof education and religion which would hold fifty people. These were the people who were agitating in the cause of dispensing with religion in the day schools. In Warrington the Church of England schools provided accommodation for 7,667, Roman Catholic for 2,693 British for .2,317,, and Wesleyan for 989. The Education Act was not a Churchmen's Act, but they thought it might be some settlement of the difficulty and they therefore sub- mitted to it. Canon MORLEY STEVENSON delivered an •address in which he reviewed the position locally. He said the Church of England had done her level best to give in her day schools fairly and squarely the teaching of the Church of England, but at tie same time to give it in such a way as had not been capable of drawing off the children from any other faith to which their parents might belong or of trying to proselytise them. He I would be glad to hear if anybody could say the con- trary to that, because he did not think the contrary could be said. He did not believe that in Warrington they could find half a dozen children who by the teach- • jug they had received in the daS7 schools of the Church of England had been drawn from any denomination to which ,they belonged or attracted from their own I Sunday school or anything of the kind. He believed Mr. Birrell was fair minded, just and honourable. and , he did not think he wanted to take any mean advantage ;of Churchpeople. But Mr. Birrell was not alone. lie had behind him a large number of people who held very strong views on the subject which were not favourable to the Church of England. Consequently he thought a I very strong effect would be made in the House .of , Commons—he did not say by Mr. Birrell or the Cabinet, but by a large number of members—to make the Bill about as bad for Church people as they could make it. Canon Stevenson deprecated the proposal that an uncle- nominational system should be introduced. Continuing, ,he said Lord Stanley of Alderley had said that if the trust deed of a school said it was built for purposes of education, then the State had a perfect , right to take that school and use it always as a school without any rent, remuneration, or acknowledgement to the people who built it. It seemed to him (Canon Stevenson) that a more monstrously unjust thin'. was never said. The schools were built in order that dis- tinctive religious teaching Might be given in them, and Lord Stanley's suggestion revolted the feeling of justice and straightforwardness that English people possessed. (Applause.) Canon Stevenson arguad that there should be no difficulty in teaching all children the religious beliefs of their parents, and said that when the two new Council schools were erected in Warrington there would be no parent in the town who could not find within a reasonable distance of his home a school in whidh his child might be taught in accordance with his own religious convictions, be they Church of England, Nonconformists or Roman Catholic. He asked if that would not be a fairer thing than to say " We shall have this undenominational teaching, which is congenial to the Nonconformist, in every school in the town, whether they like it or not." If they were going to try and force on the country by the tyranny of an enormous majority one particular kind of religious teaching and try and make it fit all sorts of people they would never have peace. They would have discontent and, they would have people always uncomfortable

'because they would feel they had not got what was just and right. (Applause). The resolution was unanimously carried. Mr, H. COLLIN moved and Mr. Panics seconded the following resolution : "As members of the Church of England, parents of children actually attending ele- mentary schools, we desire that our children shall receive in the day school instruction in the doctrines and principles of the Church of England." In supporting the Rev. W. BRACECIMP urged his hearers not to allow the trust deeds of their schools to be violated. He contended the Nonconformists had not to pay a penny rate for the teaching of religious know- ledge in church schools, as the use of the buildings free of charge was ample payment for the privilege of giving that instruction. Since 1902 they had spent £llBl 17s. 9d. on St. Paul's schools. Yet the passive resisters said the Act of 1902 was a parsons' act. On the contrary it had robbed them of a great deal of their rights and the parson was now practically no one in his schools. The resolution was unanimously passed.

div.head: Meeting in the National Schools.
div.p: Meeting in the National Schools.

Mr. R. T. Fairclough presided at a meeting of parents and others held in the National schools, Church-street, on Thursday evening. He was supported on the plat- form by the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis), Rev. T. A.. 1. Ridpath. Councillor Craik, Messrs. S. Taylor, S. Davies, and G. Brown.

The CHAIRMAN in referring to the Church's work for education in that parish said that estimating the cost of school buildings at£l2 per head—the EducationContruit- tee's estimate for the new schools—theivalue of the land at £3 per head,and furniture, &c., at £2 per head, the total value of the National schools was 217 per head. They educated over 1,000 children so he contended the value of the schools to Warrington was £17,000. When they considered what Churchpeople had expended on schools it seemed to him a great shame if they were to be interfered with by the Government. They could not too strongly protest against anything that would be to the detriment of their schools. What had the passive resisters done for education? He could not find out that they did anything, but when they were asked to pay something towards the rates their consciences would not allow them. In his opinion Churchpeople were not only paying for their own children's education but they were also paying in rates to educate the passive resisters' children. (Applause.) Mr. S. TAYLOR moved the usual resolution protest- ing against interference with definite religious teaching in schools by teachers who believed what they taught. He said the present Govern- ment—which had turned out of dike an excellent Government—had already made mistakes but if they interfered with the Church and her schools they would make such a great mistake as they would never get over. He believed they would have to go to the country on the question. It wag hinted that special treatmlimt would be given to Roman Catholics. That was all a bait to get votes. Roman Catholics were nearly all Liberals and the Government must not offend them. They could offend Churohpeople because they were opponents. Mr. S. DAVIES seconded and said that if Church- people and Roman Catholics had, before the election, known what they knew now, he questioned very much whether the Government would have been returned at all. (Applause.) Most certainly they would not have been returned with anything like their present majority. The Government had no mandate to introduce a Bill to interfere with the Church Schools. If their majority was analysed it would be found that if they appealed to the country next week they would not get more than sixty of a majority. The House of Lords would there- fore be justified in rejecting the measure, and Church- people ought by every means to strengthen the hands of the House of Lords and force the Government to appeal to the country. (Applause.) The Rev. T. A. J. RIDPATII supported. He said that in Australia the various States had seen their mistake and had abandoned purely secular education, and thoughtful authorities in America were turning their eyes towards religious education as being the one hope of that country. Churchpeople, he contended, ought years ago to have gone in for the teaching of their own form of Christianity in the Board Schools to which they so largely contributed. Mr. G. BROWN and Mr. F. G. TAYLOR also supported. The latter remarked that he did not believe the Roman Catholics were desirous of preferential treatment as was shown by the speech mace in Liverpool by a prominent member of that body. Canon MORLEY STEVENSON delivered a vigorous address. He said the bast men in America, where there was as a rule no religious teaching in schools, were de- ploring the state of things in that country—that morality and the conduct of the people were going steadily down—and unless they did something to pre- vent it the condition of affairs would become very dis- astrous indeed. They did not want that in England. If, said Canon Stevenson, the Government tried to force upon them an undenominational system, to tear up their trust deeds or, as Lord Stanley of Alderley had suggested, to take away the schools without any re- numeration, the funny little comedy of passive resist- ance would be hots. farthing dip in comparison with the great lamp which would be lighted from one end of the country to the other. (Applause.) The resolution was unanimously carried.

div.head: PROSPEROUS ASSURANCE
div.p: A PROSPEROUS ASSURANCE
COMPANY.
Good Year for the Prudential.

11 The continued remarkable prosperity of the Prudential Assurance Company Limited, is strikingly evidenced by the report on the past year's work, a summary of which is published in another oolumn. The magnitude of the concern and the far-reaching character of its operations give t. • a claim to special attention, and the report embodies many features of great interest. The total premiums received during 1905 exceeded those of the preceding year Ivy £159,715 and as showing the increased popularity of the company it is important to note that the new business exceeded £7,200,000. The Directors have decided upon removing and transferring the sum of £750,000 from the reserve fund and placing it back smcaalgenitthuede, sybstuetm it which is merely developing into the life assurance fund of the Industrial Branch. rpoaralleledin Directors n a larger have always pursued. The new departure will Thi This is enable the Directors to increase the sum assured under Table Ain the Industrial Branch by 2i per cent. and , this increase will eventually affect 13,000,000 policies, or nearly one third of the population of Great Britain and Ireland. Ten million policies will receive an immediate increase and the others as time goes on. The, deduction of £750,000, which is the estimated cost of this concession, from the reserve will still leave £1,000,000 in that fund, which is adequate for the purpose of the fund. Progress is I recorded in every department. In the Ordin- ary Branch the policies issued last year were 75,293, as against 71,871 in 1901, assuring the sum of £7,211,427 as against £6,954,650, and producing a pre- mium income of £395,029 as against £377,587. In the Industrial Branch tho increase in the premiums was £159,715 over the previous year, being a larger increase by £20,000 than that obtained in 1904. The number of policies in force at the end of the year was 16,095,298 as against 15,577,161. The results achieved speak volumes for the able management of the com- pany which still maintains its commanding position in the assurance world and bids fair li to achieve even greater prosperity in the future. We need only point to the substantial financial resources of the concern to show that the working-man possesses the amplest security for the payment of his policy at death ; while the system of Free Assurances confers a great benefit by preserving (in the form of a paid-up policy) the savings which he has already invested in the Company, should unfortunate circumstances comet him to cease the payment of further premiums. How this provision is appreciated is evident from the fact that during the past year, 123,589 policies of this character were granted. Enterprise and success are the key-notes of the Prudential, and the people are not slow to realize the real advantages offered by insuring in this great concern. The local superintendent is Mr. J. T. Rowlands, Sankey-street.

div.head: Baptist Church, Go!borne Street.
div.p: Baptist Church, Go!borne Street.

The first of a series of special sermons were given in the above church on Sunday last by the Rev. H. Dunnico. There were large congregations at both services, notwithstanding the inclement weather, the building being crowded in the evening. At the morning service Mr. Donnie° gave an introductory sermon upon " Religious Belief" pointing out that man by nature was a religious being and that all those intuitions em- bedded in the constitution of man were based up on truth. In the evening Mr. Donnie° based his discourse on the words" By their Fruits ye shall know them."

Lecture on the Holy Land. A highly interesting lecture on the Holy Land was delivered in Golborne-street Baptist Church on Thurs- day evening by Mr. J. K. Slater, of Liverpool, modera- tor of the Lancashire and Cheshire Baptist Union. The Rev. Herbert Dunnico presided over a large attendance. The lecture was splendidly illustrated with limelight views, and proved a vivid description of the tour which Sl Mr. ater enjoyed through the Holy Land. Pictures of the places with the most sacred associations were thrown on the screen, and the meeting was kept deeply interested.—At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, on the proposition of Mr. Freeman, seconded by Mr. Jones.

The New Testament. The second of a series of lectures on The New Testa- ment was delivered by the Rev. Charles Hargrove, M.A., of Leeds,in the Cairo-street Schools, on Thursday evening. There was a large attendance. The lecturer dealt with the " First three gospels and their origin." He explained that in the early years of the Christian era Christianity was not contained in a book. It was a living thing and was spoken not written. No doubt the transition from a gospel written in the hearts of men to a gospel written as we knew it was gradual. With the early Christians the existence of future generations was not thought of and it was not until his genera- tion were passing away that Mark thought it was time that the Word should be put into writing. Matthew followed with his Gospel. Luke's Gospel was evidently the latest of the three and was a literary composition which the others were not. In it was included almost the whole of the Gospel of Mark, and Luke also made use of the sayings and teachings of Jesus as given by Matthew. There was no sacredness attributed to the Gospels in those days and as efforts were made to per- fect them many variations of the Gospels came into existence.—Next week Mr. Hargrove will lecture on "The Fourth Gospel: Its authorship and historic value."

Wycliffe Church Renovation. A meeting was held In the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings on Thursday evening to consider the question ot the renovation and the repair of the Church. The Rev. John Yonge presided over a large and representa- tive gathering. Mr. E. Garland, hon. secretary of the Renovation Committee, pointed out that it was 10 years since the interior of the Church was decorated. Estimates had been obtained of the probable cost of the scheme as projected, and in round figures, amounted to £9OO. The various items in the estimates had been considered and the committee did not see how it would be possible to carry out the work satisfactorily at a less cost. So far £350 had been promised leaving £550 still to be raised, and he, for one, did not despair of that amount being forthcoming if all would have a share in raising it, especially as the £350 had been promised by 83 persons. The committee confidently appealed for the sum necessary to carry out th( work. Hitherto when occasion had demanded a special effort there had been been . a ready response and the committee appealed to the congregation ribt to be behind on this occasion.—On the motion of Mr. J. W. Slack, seconded by Mr. Edward Wallington, and supported by Messrs G. Wallington, W. Beswick; J. Longland, G. Brown, C. Eccles and J. Hawthorn, the following resolution was unanimously approved: " That, having heard the statement of the Committee as to the cost of cleaning and renovating the Chureh, this meeting pledges itself to use every effort to raise the amount required during the next twelve months, but that the commence- ment of the work he deferred until at least two-thirds of the amount required is promised."-- Various suggestions as to the method of raising the money werermade, but it was generally felt desirable if possible, to rely solely upon subscriptions.—During the evening refreshments were provided, and music%l items were given by Mr. J. W. Barnes' Miss A. Beswick, Mrs. H. Haviour, Mr. N. Cook and Mr. B. Hibbert.—Votes of thanks were passed to Mr. and Mrs. Ziba Armitage for providing the refreshments, and to the ladies and .gentlemen who had assisted in the proceedings.—The catering was in the hands of Mr. and Mrs. Atkinson, and gave every satisfaction.

ELECTRIC LIGHTING. £7,000 REQUIRED FOR MAIN EXTENSIONS AT WARRINGTON. An inquiry was conducted at the Town Hall on Wed- nesday by Mr. H. Percy Boulnois, M. Inst., C.E., an Inspector of the Local Government Board, into the application of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £lO,OOO for extension of electrical mains in the borough. Mr. T. H. Spinks (assistant CO the Town Clerk) made the application on behalf of the Corporation, and amongst those present were :—Aldermen Bennett and Smethurst, Councillors Pemberton and Skelland, Messrs. IL Thornton, C. Gough, \V. Roberts, E. England, T. Woolhouse, J. E. Richardson, R. W. Cook, and others. with Messrs. J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer). F. V. L. !Matthias (electrical engineer), F. W. Purse (assistant electrical engineer). Mr. Spinks said the application was made in deference to the opinion expressed by an inspector of the Board that the Corporation should anticipate their require- ments for a period of about three years and apply to the Board in order to avoid frequent inquiries and any excess expenditure before receiving the sanction of the Board. The Electricity Committee at a meeting on Tuesday decided to reduce theapplication from £lO,OOO to £7,000 if the Board would allow them t ) do so. The Borough Treasurer in presenting the usual statistics to the inspector, said the total indebtedness of the borough on March Ist was .21,176,355 and against that there was in the sinking fund £19,493. The amount outstanding on the electriaal undertaking on March Ist was £77,175 and the amount in the sinking fund was £1,512. The accounts for the past year showed a net profit of £1,543 12s. 91. and there was a reserve fund of £1,873 75. to meet any contingencies. Mr. S. GOUGH was about to ask some questions when the Inspector inquired if he was a member of the Council. Mr. GOCGIT : No. (Later) I should say Yes. He was proceeding to make further remarks when the Insnector said he could not go into that matter. Mr. S. Gough : What is the overdraft at the bank? The Borough Treasurer : On Saturday last it was £2.236 Is. Mr. Gough : Do you mean that the total indebted- ness of the borough is only £1,170,385 ? The Borough Treasurer : I don't like to be asked questions like this. I have given you the total indebted- ness of the borough and I don't like to have the figures questioned. When I give a statement to an Inspector of the Local Government Board, I think everybody ought to know that I would never attempt in any way to mis- lead and make a wrong statement. I protest against the question. Mr. Gough : I only wanted you to confirm the figures Continuing he asked if it was within their knowledge that the electric light that was to be supplied to some manufacturers was going to be sold at a reduced rate. The Inspector : I don't think an officer of the Cor- poration can answer that. It is a question of the policy of the Corporation. • Mr. Henry Thornton said he appeared on behalf of the Property Owners' Association, but on learning that the amount of the application had been reduced to £7,000 he said his task was considerably lightened. Had the £lO.OOO been applied for he would have had to opoose it most strenuously. Mr. F. V. L. Matthias, electrical engineer, said that of the amount applied for £1,400 was required for services and £5,800 for mains. if the demand for light and power continued at the same rateals hitherto the loan would suffice for two years. The Private con- sumers on the main were a very small proportion, but they had many big service supplies which entailed con- siderable expenditure. 'he layieg of the additional mains would not make it necessary as yet to have more plant. The Inspector: I suppose, you and your Council wish it would, because that would mean more business. From your knowledge of the working since March 31st 1905 can you say that the net income that will be produced from the past year's work will be more or less than it was for 1905? Mr. Matthias : it should be more. Mrahornton asked if it were proposed to intreduse supply to an outlying, place at an extra cost which would not recoup the Corporation? Mr.:Matthias said that according tolthe.present'scheme they were carrying oust extensions in the Wilderspool direction.iThe matter was placed before the Committee and guarantees were obtained from the firms which were going to be supplied. The Committee considered the scheme a sound one. The Inspector : T take it that yen generally advice the Committee as to these extensions and the possible recoupment. Mr. !Matthias : Yes. The inspector : There is no favour shown to any- body, that you are aware of ? Mr. Matthias : No. None at -IMr. Gough : Is any firm up Wilderspool Causeway to be supplied at a cheaper rate than the general customers ? Mr. IM.tthias : No. Councillor Pemberton : Didn't you tell us at the Electricity Committee meeting that £7,000 would be necessary in the first instance ? Mr. Matthias said he did not think so. He believed he had estimated it at £lO,OOO all along. Councillor Pemberton: lam not against the £7,000 loan. The inspeetor : The Council are not likely to borrow money unless they want it. They simply want powers, but they are not likely to borrow it all immediately. Councillor Pemberton : Unfortunately that is not our experience. The Inspector : They will have to aecount to the Board as to how they spend it. Councillor Pemberton : We had an inquiry not long ago where the money had been spent seven years before the application was made. The Inspector: it was very wrong indeed In reply to Mr. J. E. Richardson. Mr. Matthias said mains were being constructed in the Latchford direction. The estimated cost was £750 and up-to-date £5OO had been spent. The work was almost completed. Mr. Richardson : Are there a large number of peonle using the current on that length ? Mr. Matthias: Not a large number, but we are getting applications in. Mr. Richardson : Have you convinced the Council that the applications are such as will make a fair return on the capital ? Mr. Matthias : Yes. Mr. Richardson: Is the Bolton school included in the applications ? Mr. Matthias : Yes. Mr:Spinks Pointed out that the Latchford extension was not included in the application. The Inspector said the questions tended to Show whether the Council were carrying out mains that were profitable. Mr. Richardson : I take it that evidence has been given to the Council that the Latchford extension will pay its way and that there are sufficient applicants to recoup them. Mr. Matthias : Yes. , Alderman Smethurst, as chairman of the Electricity Committee, supported the application. He could assure , the inspector that he wished to be quite as economical in dealing with the money as any gentlemen present. He pointed out that the extension was necessary to meet the requirements of large customers. They had now something like 71 power customers varying in their demands from half a horse power to nearly 400 horse power. The committee were bound to move in tke matter, one of the reasons being that a large works at Wilderspool would only give them so many weeks in which to arrange the supply. He was satisfied that the committee had worked as economically as possible,' but before they handed anything to the rates he thought they should have a reserve fund of £5,000. The inquiry then closed.

"The funny little comedy of passive resistance will be but a farthing dip in comparison with the great lamp which will be lighted from one end of the country to the other if undenominational education is adopted." So says Canon Morly Stevenson. * Elementary school teachers under 35 years of age who are not already possessed of a certificate qualify- ing them to give instruction in physical exercises are required to obtain such qualification not later than July, 1907. So runs a recent order of the School Management Committee. We are obviously tending towards the time when a certain standard of muscular, as well as mental, development will be required of the elementary school teacher. Then, woe betide the lazy or cheeky scholar!

Deslandres recorded two about the same time. LIQUID CRYSTALS. Referring to a book published on liquid cry stals by Dr. Rudolf Schenck, the Globe says: To most people the word "liquid-crystal" will ap- pear a contradiction in terms, for the most essen- tial point about a crystal is that it is a definite geometrical solid, bounded by plane faces. It must be remembered, however, that crystals pos- sess other essential properties, and that liquids may possess these without the definite outward form. When, some years ace. Professor Leh- mann announced the discovery of liquid crystals. the announcement was received with a good deal of doubt. The discovery, however, was soon confirmed by other workers, and especially by Dr. Schenck, the author of the above work. In defence of the view that these liquids with the OPTIAL PROPERTIES OF CRYSTALS 'should really be classed as crystals. it was urged that there was a gradual transition between the ordinary crystal which retains its shape under considerable pressure, and the liquid with the optical properties. but not the shape of the cry- stal. A cube of fluc,r-spar, for example, offers considerable resistance to deformation, while a crystal of yellow phosphorus is quite soft. In the case of the liquid crystals, the rigidity has be- come so slight that, when placed in a liquid of equal density, they assume a spherical form. A slight rise of temperature causes the linuid cry- stal to Pass into the form of an ordinary liquid. It would, perhaps, be more philosophical to look upon liquid crystals as intermediate bodies possessing some, but not all, the prsperties of true crystals. In this connection, the remark- able experiments of Dr. Renitzer, of Pragtho, on substances with TWO MELTING POINTS must be mentioned. He found that benzoate of colesteryl melted at 145 deg. to a dull doubly-re- fractive liquid—that is. a liquid with crystalline properties—and at 178 deg. to a clear liquid not nossessing such properties. Another substance, known as Azoxyphenol. meltod tr, limiid which actually retained the !mane as wen as MO OptICSI properties of the crystal at a temperature of 134 deg., while at 165 deg. it passed into as ordi- nary liauid.

THE HEARING OF FISHES. In discussing the question whether fish can hear or not, Professor Korner lays stress on the argument that hearing would be a superfluous sense for them. They possess, he points out, such keen powers of sight, smell, and touch that it is improbable that the sense of hearing should be also developed. Again, there is good reason for believing that the so-called organs of Corti are the sole means in mammals by which sound is received and transmitted to the brain. And these organs are absent in fishes. An incidental argument is afforded by the fact that numbers of sharks were present at the battle of Aboukir Bay and other naval engagements, and went about their usual business in spite of the roar of the cannons. According to Propessor Korner, again, while fish are able to take cognisance of vibrations communicated to the water by an electric bell, they take no notice of a single loud explosion under water, such as that made by dynamite. Brehm's anecdote of the carp in the pond corning to the landing-stage to be fed at the sound of a bell may be explained by sup- posing that the fish feel the vibrations of the footsteps of the persons coming to the pond.
